lessons.title: Read a vector

steps.headline: Directions as a pair of numbers

lead.text: Start with the café, 4 blocks east and 1 block north of where you stand. On a map east runs across the page and north runs up it, so the café's directions are 4 across and 1 up. Every direction of this kind has the same two parts, which means we can drop the words and keep the numbers: (4, 1). The first number says how far across to go and the second says how far up.

Each number in the pair is called a coordinate. We name them with letters: the across number is x and the up number is y, so in (4, 1) we have x = 4 and y = 1. A pair of numbers written in a fixed order like this is called a vector. You can picture it as an arrow that starts where you stand and ends at the café.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the café's vector and, for comparison, a library at (2, 3). Switch between them and watch where each arrow ends. Across always comes first and up always comes second, so reading a vector comes down to knowing which position you are looking at.

lead.text: The café is at (4, 1), as before. A bank is at (1, 4), which means 1 block east and 4 blocks north. Both are measured from where you stand.

reveal.text: The café's across number is 4 and the bank's is 1. Only the first numbers describe east and west, so those are the ones to compare.

lead.text: So far every number has been positive, because the café lies east and north of you. Places do not always lie that way. A kiosk might be 3 blocks west of you and 2 blocks north. Rather than invent new words, we put a minus sign on the number: a negative across number means left, and a negative up number means down.

The kiosk is at (−3, 2). Its x coordinate is −3, which is 3 to the left, and its y coordinate is 2, which is 2 up. A fountain 5 blocks east and 1 block south would be (5, −1), because south is down and down is negative.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the kiosk's arrow starts at the same corner as before and heads left as it climbs. The sign belongs to the number it sits in front of. It does not change which position the number is in, so the first number is still x and the second is still y, whatever their signs.

steps.headline: Read the vector (−4, 1): what are x and y?

workedSteps.text: The pair is written (x, y), so x is the first number. Its minus sign stays with it, so x means 4 to the left.
y is the second number. It has no minus sign, so it means 1 up.

lead.text: Decide which of the two numbers the question asks about before you answer, and keep its sign if it has one.

reveal.text: You read x straight from the first position. The −2 is y, and it sends the arrow down.

lead.text: Take the pairs (2, 6) and (6, 2). They use the same two numbers, yet (2, 6) means 2 across and 6 up, and (6, 2) means 6 across and 2 up. One ends high above the starting point and the other ends far along to the side. Two vectors are the same only when their coordinates match in every position, so swapping the numbers gives a different vector.

A pair can also hold a zero. The pair (5, 0) goes 5 across and no distance up, so it runs along the ground. A zero in a position means there is no movement in that direction. A pair that is zero in both positions has a name of its own, the zero vector, and it is written (0, 0).

workedSteps.text: Write each pair as (x, y).
Compare the x coordinates, then the y coordinates. Are the vectors the same?

lead.text: Read each number as an instruction, the way you read the café's directions.

reveal.text: You read each zero as an instruction to stay put. Zero across and zero up is no movement at all, so the zero vector marks the starting point itself.

lead.text: So far each pair has been the address of a place, measured from where you stand. A vector has a second use: it can describe a move, a change from wherever you happen to be. The directions 'go 3 across and 4 up' make sense from any corner of the grid, and they always add the same 3 and 4 to wherever you started.

A robot on a factory floor shows the idea. Its controller sends a move such as (3, 4), and the robot reads it exactly as you read the café's directions: the first number is how far across and the second is how far up. A robot that starts somewhere else follows the same move and ends somewhere else, but the move itself stays the same.
Seen this way a vector is an instruction about a change. That is why two of them can be put one after the other to make a single longer move, which the next lesson works out.
A factory robot is told its next move as a vector (across, up). The move (2, 5) would send it 2 across and 5 up.

blocks.text: You are standing in a town laid out on a grid, and a friend asks how to reach a café. You could draw a map, or you could say 'walk 4 blocks east, then 1 block north'. Directions like that carry everything your friend needs, and the same style of directions describes how a boat is steered or how a character moves across a game screen.

Writing them out takes a lot of words. A bank 1 block east and 4 blocks north needs another sentence, and a delivery driver might need fifty. Mathematicians shortened directions to a pair of numbers, and that pair is one of the simplest objects in linear algebra, the subject of this course.
This lesson shows how to read such a pair. We begin with the café, learn what each number says, work out what a minus sign does, and finish by seeing why the order of the two numbers matters.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a pair of directions with its signs and say why swapping the two numbers gives a different place.

recap.keyIdea: A vector is an ordered list of coordinates: across first, then up. Swap the numbers and you have a different vector.

blocks.text: Back at the café, you can now give its directions as two numbers. You read x and y from pairs with minus signs, showed that (1, 4) and (4, 1) are different vectors, and saw that the zero vector leaves you where you began.

recap.nextHook: A vector is a move, so two moves can follow one another. The next lesson starts with a walk of two legs and works out where it ends.

lessons.title: Add and scale vectors

lead.text: Take a courier's trip in two legs. The first leg is (3, 1), which is 3 across and 1 up. The second leg is (2, 2). To find where she ends up, add up everything she moved across and everything she moved up. Across she moved 3 and then 2, which makes 5. Up she moved 1 and then 2, which makes 3.

The whole trip comes to (5, 3), which we write as the sum (3, 1) + (2, 2) = (5, 3). Adding two vectors means adding their across numbers to each other and their up numbers to each other. Across and up never mix. A block east tells you nothing about how far north you went.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the second arrow starts where the first one stops, and the sum is the single arrow from the start to the finish. Switch to the other case and see what a backward leg does: a negative number pulls the finish back with it.

lead.text: A second courier makes the legs (2, 1) and (−1, 3), both measured in blocks. Follow her legs one after the other.

reveal.text: You added only the north parts, 1 and 3. Vectors add one coordinate at a time.

lead.text: Suppose the courier's stops are at (7, 5) and (2, 1), measured from the depot. To find the walk from the second stop to the first, subtract the vectors. Take the across numbers away from each other and the up numbers away from each other: (7, 5) − (2, 1) = (7 − 2, 5 − 1) = (5, 4). The first vector comes first, so the order of the subtraction matters.

Subtraction works one coordinate at a time, just as addition does. It also explains how one leg can cancel another. A walk of (4, 1) followed by (−4, −1) leaves you where you began, because each pair of coordinates adds to zero. The second walk is the opposite of the first, and an opposite is found by changing the sign of every coordinate. Subtracting a vector gives the same result as adding its opposite.

A courier who makes the same delivery run three times walks the leg (1, 2) three times. Adding the legs gives (1 + 1 + 1, 2 + 2 + 2) = (3, 6). That is the same as multiplying each coordinate by 3, so we write it as three times the vector: 3(1, 2) = (3, 6).

A plain number used to stretch or shrink a vector is called a scalar, and multiplying a vector by one is called scaling. Every coordinate is multiplied by the same scalar, because scaling stretches the whole arrow and does not bend it. A scalar of 3 makes the arrow three times as long, pointing the same way. A scalar of one half makes it half as long.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the scalar changes how long the arrow is and leaves the direction alone.

workedSteps.text: Multiply every coordinate by 3. The x coordinate first.
Now the y coordinate.

lead.text: A scalar can be negative. Multiply by −1 and every coordinate changes sign, so (1, 2) becomes (−1, −2). The arrow has the same length as before and points the opposite way, like the courier turning round to walk the same leg backwards.

A larger negative scalar does two jobs at once. Multiplying by −3 stretches the arrow to three times its length and flips it round: (1, 2) becomes (−3, −6). Each coordinate is still multiplied, and the minus sign is part of the number. When a coordinate is already negative, a negative scalar makes it positive, so −2 × (−3) = 6.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows both cases: a flip alone, and a flip with a stretch.

lead.text: Multiply each coordinate by the scalar and keep its sign. Only the first coordinate is needed.

reveal.text: You multiplied by a negative number, so the coordinate changed sign as well as size. That is the flip.

lead.text: Real journeys mix both operations. A courier might make the leg (1, 3) twice and then add a final stretch of (4, −2). Written as one expression, that is 2(1, 3) + (4, −2). Ordinary arithmetic decides the order: the scaling is done first, and then the vectors are added.

Scaling gives (2, 6). Adding (4, −2) coordinate by coordinate gives (2 + 4, 6 − 2) = (6, 4). A sum of scaled vectors like this is called a combination of the vectors. Later lessons use combinations to describe every place a set of vectors can reach.

workedSteps.text: Scale first. Multiply both coordinates by 2.
Now add matching coordinates.

lead.text: A drone's flights are vectors (across, up). Two flights in a row add in the same way as the legs of the courier's trip.

blocks.text: A courier is making a delivery on a town grid. She leaves the depot, walks 2 blocks east and 1 block north to collect a parcel, then walks 1 block west and 3 blocks north to the customer's door. Each leg of the trip is a pair of numbers of the kind you met in the last lesson, so the whole trip is two vectors, one after the other.

The depot manager only wants to know where she ended up. Following both legs on a map works, but it is slow. If the two pairs could be combined into one, the manager could skip the map, and a single pair could stand in for a trip of any number of legs.
This lesson finds out how to combine vectors. We start with joining two legs, move on to taking a leg back and to repeating one, and finish by building a route out of several pieces.

intro.promise: By the end you'll add and subtract vectors and multiply one by a number, working one coordinate at a time.

recap.keyIdea: Vectors add and subtract coordinate by coordinate. A scalar multiplies every coordinate, and a negative scalar also reverses the direction.

blocks.text: Back with the courier, you worked out where a two-leg trip ends by adding coordinates. You tripled a leg, flipped one with a negative scalar, and put scaling and adding together in a single expression.

recap.nextHook: You can now say where a route ends. The next lesson asks how long the straight shortcut from start to finish is, and that takes a new kind of product.

lessons.title: Dot products and length

lead.text: Take a smaller field to check the idea, one that is 8 m across and 15 m up. The two sides you would walk meet at a right angle, and the straight line between the corners is the long side of the triangle they make. Pythagoras's rule says that the square on the long side equals the sum of the squares on the two short sides.

Squaring the sides gives 8² + 15² = 64 + 225 = 289, so the shortcut is the square root of 289, which is 17 m. The same recipe finds the length of any vector (x, y). Square each coordinate and add the two squares. The square root of that total is the length of the vector, and it is never negative.

afterFigure.text: The picture draws each vector as the long side of a right-angled triangle. Turning the field round, from (8, 15) to (15, 8), gives a different vector with the same length, because the same two squares are added.

lead.text: The walk from one corner of the field to the opposite corner is a vector: 9 across and 12 up.

reveal.text: You squared 9 and 12 and added the squares, then took the square root. That recipe gives the length of any vector.

lead.text: The sum of squares follows a pattern. Each coordinate is multiplied by itself and the two results are added. The same pattern works on two different vectors. Take (2, 5) and (1, 3). Multiply the across numbers together and the up numbers together. Then add the two products: 2 × 1 + 5 × 3 = 17.
This is called the dot product. We write it with a dot between the vectors, so (2, 5) · (1, 3) = 17. The answer is one number, a scalar with no across and up parts.

Now put the same vector on both sides of the dot. The dot product of (8, 15) with itself is 8 × 8 + 15 × 15 = 289, exactly the number you added up to find the length. A vector's dot product with itself is its length squared, so its length is the square root of that dot product.
Multiply matching coordinates and add the products. The answer is a single number.

reveal.text: You multiplied 1 × 3 and 2 × 4, then added 3 and 8. A dot product always ends as one number.

lead.text: Coordinates can be negative, so it is worth checking what a minus sign does. A length squares each coordinate first, and a negative number times itself is positive: (−8)² = 64, the same as 8². The vectors (8, 15) and (−8, 15) end up with the same length, 17. Length ignores direction.

In a dot product the signs matter more. A positive number times a negative one gives a negative product, and the two products can pull against each other. For (3, 1) · (−2, 5) the products are −6 and 5, which add to −1. A dot product can come out negative. A vector dotted with itself cannot, since each of its products is a number times itself.

workedSteps.text: Square each coordinate and add. This is the vector's dot product with itself.
Add the squares.
The length is the positive square root.
Multiply matching coordinates.
Add the two products. What is the dot product?

lead.text: Dot a vector with itself and every product is a number times itself. Keep the signs as you go.

reveal.text: Each product was a number times itself, so both came out positive. A vector's dot product with itself is never negative.

lead.text: A vector built from a journey has a second reading. The pair (across, up) says which way a traveller went from her start. Its length says how far from the start she ended up in a straight line, whatever route she took. With coordinates in kilometres, the length comes out in kilometres too, since the square root undoes the squaring and returns the unit.

A hiker whose displacement is (−8, −15) kilometres has gone 8 km west and 15 km south. Her distance from the start is √(64 + 225) = 17 km. The path she took may have been longer. The vector only records where she ended up, so its length is the distance a bird would fly.
A hiker's displacement is a vector in kilometres, (across, up). Her distance from the start is the length of that vector.

blocks.text: A rectangular field is 9 m wide and 12 m long. You stand at one corner and want to reach the opposite one. You can walk along two sides, which is 9 m and then 12 m, so 21 m in all. A gap in the hedge lets you cut straight across, and the straight line is clearly shorter.

How much shorter depends on a rule you may remember from school, and the rule belongs to vectors. The walk to the far corner is the vector (9, 12), which is 9 across and 12 up. Its length is the distance of the straight route.
This lesson finds the length of a vector from its coordinates. Along the way we meet a new way of combining two vectors that gives a single number and has a length hidden inside it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a vector's length from its coordinates and calculate the dot product of two vectors.

recap.keyIdea: The dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds the products into one number. A vector's dot product with itself is its squared length.

blocks.text: Back at the field, you can now say how long the shortcut is from its sides alone. You found that (2, 1) · (3, −2) = 4, that (−7, 24) is 25 long, and that a minus sign cannot change a length because squaring removes it.

recap.nextHook: You can now measure any vector. The next lesson shrinks a 10 m step to exactly 1 m in the same direction, and finds out what it means when a dot product comes to zero.

lessons.title: Orthogonal and unit vectors

lead.text: Start with a simple case. The vector (0, 10) is 10 m long, and (0, 1) points the same way with length 1. We got from one to the other by dividing every coordinate by 10, which is the length. Dividing by a number shrinks the arrow without turning it, because every coordinate shrinks by the same factor.

Any vector works the same way. Take (8, 15), whose length is 17 from the last lesson. Dividing both coordinates by 17 gives (8/17, 15/17). Check the new length: (8/17)² + (15/17)² = 64/289 + 225/289 = 289/289 = 1.

A vector of length 1 is called a unit vector. Dividing a vector by its own length is called normalising it. The result points the same way as the original, so a unit vector records a direction and nothing else.
Back to the step of (6, 8) metres, which is 10 m long. You want a step in exactly the same direction that is only 1 m long.

reveal.text: You scaled the step by one over its length. Multiplying by that number leaves the direction alone and brings the length to 1.

workedSteps.text: Find the length.
Divide every coordinate by the length.

steps.headline: Find the x coordinate of the unit vector in the direction (3, 4).

workedSteps.text: Find the length.
Divide the x coordinate by the length. Give it as a decimal.

steps.headline: Signs, and the directions along the axes

lead.text: Dividing by the length keeps the direction. A length is never negative, so dividing a coordinate by it leaves that coordinate's sign alone. The length of (−3, 4) is 5, which gives the unit vector (−0.6, 0.8). It still points left and up.

Two unit vectors are special: (1, 0) goes straight across and (0, 1) goes straight up. Any other unit vector ends somewhere on the circle of radius 1 around the start. The next screen looks at how (1, 0) and (0, 1) relate to each other.

afterFigure.text: The picture compares (−3, 4) with its unit vector, which is the same arrow shrunk to length 1.

steps.headline: Right angles and the dot product

lead.text: The vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1) meet at a right angle, one along the ground and one straight up. The dot product can detect this: 1 × 0 + 0 × 1 = 0.

The dot product measures how much two vectors point the same way. Vectors pointing roughly the same way give a large positive number, such as (2, 0) · (3, 0) = 6. Vectors pointing opposite ways give a negative number, such as (2, 0) · (−3, 0) = −6. Vectors at a right angle share no direction at all, and their dot product is zero: (1, 0) · (0, 5) = 0.

Two vectors whose dot product is zero are called orthogonal, the word for meeting at a right angle. The test also works away from the axes. The vectors (4, 1) and (−1, 4) are orthogonal, because 4 × (−1) + 1 × 4 = 0.
Vector (1, 2) goes 1 across and 2 up. Vector (−2, 1) goes 2 to the left and 1 up. Find their dot product.

reveal.text: You found that the two products cancel. A dot product of zero means the vectors are orthogonal: the arrows meet at a right angle.

lead.text: A dot product of zero means two vectors are orthogonal. Work out the dot product of each pair in turn.

reveal.text: Only the first pair gives zero: 1 × 1 + 1 × (−1) = 0. The others give 8 and 6, so they are not at right angles.

lead.text: Both ideas can apply to one set of vectors. Take (1, 0) and (0, 1). They are orthogonal and each has length 1. A set of vectors with both properties is called orthonormal, which joins orthogonal to normalised.
Orthogonal alone is weaker. The vectors (6, 0) and (0, 4) meet at a right angle, since 6 × 0 + 0 × 4 = 0, but their lengths are 6 and 4. They pass the first test and fail the second.

To make an orthonormal pair from orthogonal vectors, divide each by its own length. Dividing keeps each direction, which keeps the right angle. Every length becomes 1. Later lessons come back to orthonormal sets as the cleanest rulers for a grid.
A game turns a velocity into a direction by dividing it by its length. A character is standing still, so its velocity is (0, 0).

blocks.text: You take a step of (6, 8) metres, which is 6 across and 8 up. By the rule from the last lesson it is 10 m long. A direction without a size is useful whenever you care where something is heading and not how far it goes, as a game does when it points a character at a door.

A second puzzle sits beside it. Two paths leave a junction, and you want to know whether they cross at a right angle. A surveyor checks this with a set square, but numbers can answer it too, and the dot product from the last lesson supplies the test.
We start with the 1 m step and then look at right angles. At the end the two ideas join into one description of the cleanest set of directions a grid can have.

lessons.title: Matrix shape and transpose

lead.text: A table of numbers is called a matrix. The numbers sit in lines of two kinds: rows go across and columns go down. Here is a matrix of prices in pounds. Each row is a shop, and each column is an item.

The first row says that shop 1 sells item 1 for 3 and item 2 for 8. The size of a matrix is its shape, written as rows × columns. This one has 3 rows and 2 columns, so its shape is 3 × 2. Always say the rows first. A 2 × 3 matrix and a 3 × 2 matrix are different shapes, even though they hold the same number of entries.
Count the rows first and then the columns, and write the shape in that order.

reveal.text: There are two rows and three columns, so the shape is 2 × 3. Rows always come first.

lead.text: Each number inside a matrix is called an entry. To point at one, give its row and then its column, counting both from 1. In the price matrix, entry (3, 1) is 9, because it sits in row 3 and column 1: the third shop's price for the first item. Entry (1, 2) is 8.

Row first and column second is the same order as the shape, and it is easy to reverse by accident. Entry (2, 1) is 5, in the second row and the first column, and it is a different number from entry (1, 2). When the matrix has a name such as A, entry (i, j) of A means the number in row i and column j.

Back to the timetable. Flipping it so that the days run down the side turns each row into a column. For a matrix this operation is called the transpose. The transpose of A is written Aᵀ, and its columns are the rows of A taken in order.

Entries travel with their rows. A number in row i and column j of A sits in row j and column i of Aᵀ. The price matrix has 3 rows and 2 columns, so its transpose has 2 rows and 3 columns. The shape swaps along with the entries.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows a 2 × 3 matrix beside its transpose. Find one entry in the original and follow it to its new position.

lead.text: Flipping swaps the two directions. Decide where each of the numbers 4 and 7 ends up.

reveal.text: The 7 periods moved from the side to the top. Flipping a table swaps rows and columns, which is what the transpose does.

lead.text: A matrix can be applied to a vector. Take one row of the matrix and multiply it by the vector in matching pairs. Then add the products. That is a dot product worked out once per row, and each row supplies one entry of the result.

Take the price matrix and the vector (1, 0). Row 1 gives 3 × 1 + 8 × 0 = 3, row 2 gives 5, and row 3 gives 9, so the result is (3, 5, 9). Each row of this matrix has 2 entries, and it pairs with a vector of 2 entries. Offer it a vector of 3 entries and the pairing runs out, because the rows have nothing for the third entry to meet.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the matrix has 2 columns, so the vector beside it has 2 entries. A matrix accepts a vector only when the vector has one entry for each of its columns.

lead.text: A has 2 rows and 3 columns, and A v pairs each row of A with v.

reveal.text: You matched the vector to a row of A. Each row is as long as the matrix has columns, so the vector needs exactly that many entries.

blocks.text: A school timetable has 4 days across the top and 7 periods down the side. Each box holds a lesson, and you find any lesson by choosing a day and a period. A teacher who prefers the days down the side can flip the whole sheet, so that rows become columns and columns become rows.

Tables of numbers turn up all over this subject. A table holds several vectors side by side, and one table can describe how a whole plane is stretched or turned. Before we use one we need to read it properly. That means knowing how big it is and how to point at a single number in it, and what flipping does to it.
This lesson turns the timetable into numbers. We name a table's size and flip it. We also find out which vectors a table fits.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find any number in a table by its row and column, and flip the table with the transpose.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix is a table with a shape of rows by columns. Its transpose swaps the two: entry (i, j) moves to position (j, i).

blocks.text: Back at the timetable, you can now say how big a table is and flip it. You found entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ and saw that applying a matrix to a vector needs one vector entry for each column.

recap.nextHook: Applying a matrix to a vector, as on the last screen, is more than arithmetic. The next lesson shows that it moves every point of the plane, and that the columns of the matrix decide where each point goes.

lessons.title: Linear transformations

lead.text: Here is the machine from the opening, written as a rule. It takes a point (x, y) and gives back a new point whose across value is 2x + y and whose up value is y. Drop in (2, 2) and the across value is 2 × 2 + 2 = 6, while the up value stays at 2. So (2, 2) comes out as (6, 2).

A rule like this is called a map, because it maps each point to another point. Look at how the rule is built. Each output value is made from x and y by multiplying them by fixed numbers and adding the results. The across value uses the numbers 2 and 1, and the up value uses 0 and 1.
Those fixed numbers are the whole machine. Change them and you have a different machine, so everything the machine does can be read from them.
Use the machine from the opening: the across value is 2x + y and the up value is y.

reveal.text: You put 3 in for x and 1 in for y: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7. Every output value of a matrix map is worked out this way.

steps.headline: Writing the rule as a matrix

lead.text: Every machine of this kind can be written as a matrix, with one row for each output value. The across value 2x + y uses the numbers 2 and 1, so the first row is (2, 1). The up value uses 0 and 1, so the second row is (0, 1).

To run the machine, dot each row with the input. The first row dotted with (x, y) gives 2x + y, and the second gives 0x + 1y, which is just y. A row dotted with the input gives one output value, and the rows together give the whole output.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows a different matrix at work. Find the row that produces each output value and check the arithmetic yourself. Whatever the matrix, the rule is the same: row i dotted with the input gives output value i.

cases.label: The same matrix and the point (2, 0)

lead.text: Here A is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and the input is v = (1, 2). Find the first output value of A v.

reveal.text: You dotted the first row with v. Each output entry has its own row, and the rows of A decide the output.

lead.text: Some maps behave better than others, and the good ones follow two simple rules. To see them, run the machine on a few points. Put in (1, 0) and it gives back (2, 0). Put in (0, 1) and it gives back (1, 1). Now put in (1, 1), which is those two inputs added together. The machine gives back (3, 1), and that is exactly (2, 0) + (1, 1).
So adding the inputs and then running the machine gives the same result as running it first and adding afterwards. Write T for the map. For any two points u and v, T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v).

The second rule is about scaling. Put in (3, 0), which is three copies of (1, 0). The machine gives back (6, 0), which is three copies of (2, 0). In symbols, T(cv) = c T(v) for any number c. A map that obeys both rules is called a linear transformation, and every matrix gives one.
Suppose T is a linear map. You scale its input v by a factor of 3.

reveal.text: You matched scaling the input to scaling the output. T(3v) is three copies of T(v).

lead.text: Scaling has a consequence for one special input. Multiplying any point by 0 gives the zero point, so T(0 × v) = 0 × T(v) = 0. A linear map always sends the zero point, the origin of the grid, to the zero point.

That gives a quick test for a map that might be linear. Drop in (0, 0) and look at what comes out. Take a machine that lifts every point two units, so (x, y) becomes (x, y + 2). Feed it (0, 0) and it returns (0, 2). Zero has moved, so the machine cannot be linear.
Passing the test proves nothing by itself, because a map can keep zero fixed and still break the sum or scaling rule. Failing it settles the matter.

Look again at the matrix with rows (2, 1) and (0, 1). The machine sent (1, 0) to (2, 0) and (0, 1) to (1, 1). Those outputs are the columns of the matrix: the first column is (2, 0) and the second is (1, 1). The reason is the zero in the input. Dotting a row with (1, 0) multiplies the row's second entry by 0, so only its first entry is left, and the first entries of the rows make up the first column.

The input (0, 1) picks out the second column in the same way. These two points sit one step along each axis, and every other point is built from them. The point (3, 2) is three copies of (1, 0) plus two copies of (0, 1). A linear map keeps sums and scaling, so its output for (3, 2) is three copies of the first output plus two copies of the second.
So the whole machine can be rebuilt from two outputs. If a linear map sends (1, 0) to (4, 1) and (0, 1) to (2, 3), then (3, 2) goes to 3 × (4, 1) + 2 × (2, 3) = (16, 9).

workedSteps.text: Dot each row with (1, 0).
The output is the first column of A.

workedSteps.text: The second output entry is the second row of A, (3, 1), dotted with the input (1, 0).
Work it out. What is the second coordinate?

lead.text: Take the first row of A and dot it with the input. Here A is $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}$ and the input is (2, 1).

reveal.text: You dotted a row with the input. Doing every row gives the whole output, one entry per row.

lead.text: A game shifts every point one unit to the right, so S(v) = v + (1, 0). Use the zero test from earlier.

blocks.text: Take a sheet of graph paper and a machine that moves points. You drop in the point (3, 1) and the machine hands back a different point. Drop in (0, 0) and you get one more. Feed it every point on the sheet and the whole grid comes back stretched, tilted or squashed into a new shape.

The last lesson ended with a matrix being applied to a vector. That matrix is a machine of this kind: the numbers in it are the rule, and the vector is the point you drop in. We will follow the machine one point at a time, to see how the rule is carried out.

Then we look for what makes a machine well behaved. Some machines turn out to be fixed completely by what they do to just two points, which is why a small table of numbers can describe a whole plane's worth of movement.

intro.promise: By the end you'll apply a matrix to a vector, and test whether a map keeps sums, scaling and the origin.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix maps a vector by dotting each of its rows with the input. A linear map keeps sums and scaling, so it keeps zero at zero, and its columns are the outputs for (1, 0) and (0, 1).

blocks.text: Back at the machine, you can now work out any output value from a row and rebuild a map from two outputs. You found that A(1, 0) is the first column and that a shift fails the zero test.

recap.nextHook: Run one machine and then another, and the two together make a third machine. The next lesson asks which single matrix does that job, and why the order the machines run in matters.

lessons.title: Compose matrix maps

lead.text: The order in which you use machines changes what comes out. Take a machine R that triples a number and a machine S that subtracts 2. Start at 4 and send it through R first: 4 becomes 12, and S then turns that into 10. Now send 4 through S first: it becomes 2, and R then turns that into 6.

The two runs end at 10 and 6, so the order matters. Running one machine on the output of another is called composing them. A composition is itself a machine, because every input still produces exactly one output. When the machines are matrices the composition has a matrix as well, called the product of the two matrices.
Two things need settling: which matrix in a written product runs first, and how to find the entries of the product. The next screens take them in that order.
Work through each run in full, then compare the two final numbers.

reveal.text: P then Q gives 5 × 2 + 3 = 13. Q then P gives (5 + 3) × 2 = 16. The same two machines in a different order end at different numbers.

lead.text: Matrices follow the same pattern. Let A and B be matrices and v a vector. Applying B to v gives the vector B v, and applying A to that gives A(B v). The product A B is the single matrix that does both jobs, so A B v means A(B v).

That fixes the order. The matrix written nearest the vector runs first, so in A B v it is B that acts first and A that acts second. It reads backwards, the way f(g(x)) means apply g first and then f. Writing B A instead gives a different machine, and the two orders usually give different results.

afterFigure.text: In the picture, A slides each point sideways by its up value and B doubles the across values. The same two matrices multiplied in opposite orders give two different products.

cases.label: A B: A slides, B doubles

lead.text: The expression A B v asks for two maps to be applied to v, one after the other.

reveal.text: You read it from the inside out. In a product of maps, the matrix nearest the vector acts first.

lead.text: To find the matrix A B, ask what it does to the two points one step along each axis. Take A with rows (1, 1) and (0, 1), and B with rows (2, 0) and (0, 1). The point (1, 0) goes through B first, and B sends it to its own first column, which is (2, 0). Then A turns (2, 0) into (2, 0).
The point (0, 1) goes to the second column of B, which is (0, 1), and A turns that into (1, 1). So the columns of A B are (2, 0) and (1, 1), and the product has rows (2, 1) and (0, 1).

Look at how each column was made: it is A applied to a column of B. Applying a matrix means dotting each of its rows with the input, so entry (i, j) of A B is row i of A dotted with column j of B. Entry (1, 2) here is (1, 1) dotted with (0, 1), which is 1.
Entry (i, j) of a product pairs one line of the left matrix with one line of the right matrix.

reveal.text: You paired a row of the left matrix with a column of the right one. The left matrix gives the row and the right matrix gives the column.

steps.headline: Compare A B v with B A v for A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 1).

workedSteps.text: B acts first, then A.
Swap the order. A acts first, then B.

steps.headline: Find entry (1, 2) of A B, for A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Entry (1, 2) uses row 1 of A, which is (1, 2), and column 2 of B, which is (0, 3).
Dot the row with the column. What is the entry?

lead.text: Let A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$. Entry (2, 1) pairs row 2 of A with column 1 of B.

reveal.text: You paired a row of A with a column of B and added the products. That is the rule for every entry of a product.

lead.text: A row can only be dotted with a column of the same length. A row of A has as many entries as A has columns, and a column of B has as many entries as B has rows. So A B exists only when A has as many columns as B has rows. These two numbers have to match.

Take A with 2 rows and 3 columns, which is a 2 × 3 matrix, and B with 3 rows and 2 columns, a 3 × 2 matrix. The inner numbers are both 3, so every row of A pairs with every column of B. The product has one entry for each row of A and each column of B, so its shape is given by the outer numbers: 2 × 2.
Swap the order and the inner numbers change. B A is 3 × 2 times 2 × 3, which also exists. Its shape is 3 × 3, a different size from A B, so the order matters here too.
Matrix A holds the prices of 3 products in 2 shops, so it is 2 × 3. Matrix B holds the sales of those 3 products in 2 months, so it is 3 × 2.
Transposing a product raises a small puzzle. The obvious guess is that (A B)ᵀ equals Aᵀ Bᵀ, and the shapes show that it cannot.

Keep A as 2 × 3 and B as 3 × 2. The product A B is 2 × 2, so (A B)ᵀ is 2 × 2 as well. Now look at Aᵀ Bᵀ. Aᵀ is 3 × 2 and Bᵀ is 2 × 3, so their product is 3 × 3. A 3 × 3 matrix cannot equal a 2 × 2 one. Reversing the order gives Bᵀ Aᵀ, which is 2 × 3 times 3 × 2. That has shape 2 × 2, as required.
The rule is (A B)ᵀ = Bᵀ Aᵀ, with the order reversed. Everyday life has the same pattern. If you put on socks and then shoes, undoing it means taking the shoes off first and the socks second.

lessons.orientation: Multiply compatible matrices and keep the order of composition.

blocks.text: Two machines sit side by side on a workbench. Machine P doubles any number you give it, and machine Q adds 3. You have the number 5, and there are two ways to use the machines. You can send it through P first and then through Q, or through Q first and then through P.

Machines on the plane work the same way. Stretch the grid with one matrix and turn it with another, and the two steps together do a single job. That raises two puzzles: whether one matrix can do both jobs at once, and whether the order of the machines matters.

This lesson settles both. We start with plain numbers to see why order can change the result. Then we move to matrices, find the single matrix that stands for two in a row, and learn the rule for working out each of its entries.

intro.promise: By the end you'll multiply two matrices entry by entry, and say which map acts first in a product.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix product is two maps in a row, and the matrix nearest the vector acts first. Entry (i, j) of A B is row i of A dotted with column j of B, and swapping the order usually changes the result.

blocks.text: Back at the two machines, you now know why the order matters. You found that entry (1, 2) of A B is 6 where B A gives 4, and that a 2 × 3 matrix times a 3 × 2 matrix gives a 2 × 2 matrix.

recap.nextHook: Two maps in a row can cancel, so that the plane ends up exactly where it began. The next lesson looks at the matrix that does nothing at all, and at the map that undoes another.

lessons.title: Identity and inverses

lead.text: Undoing a machine means reversing its steps in the opposite order. Take a machine that triples a number and then subtracts 4, and suppose it gave back 11. The last step was the subtraction, so undo that first: add 4 to get 15. The step before was the tripling, so divide by 3 to get 5. Check by running forwards: 5 tripled is 15, and 15 less 4 is 11.

This is the socks and shoes of the last lesson. To undo putting on socks and then shoes, you take off the shoes first. The reversing machine is called the inverse of the original, and for a matrix A the inverse is written A⁻¹.
Doing a machine and then its inverse leaves every input where it started. That only works if the original machine can be undone, and some cannot. We meet those later in the lesson.
Work backwards through the machine. The last step comes off first.

reveal.text: You undid the adding first and the doubling second: 17 − 3 = 14, and half of 14 is 7.

lead.text: Before looking for inverses, meet the machine that does nothing. The identity matrix has ones down its diagonal, which runs from top left to bottom right. Every other entry is zero. For two coordinates it has rows (1, 0) and (0, 1).
Dot its rows with any input (x, y) and the first row gives x back while the second gives y, so it leaves every point where it was. It is written I, and I v = v for every vector v.

afterFigure.text: The identity is also how an inverse is described. A machine followed by its inverse changes nothing, so A⁻¹ A = I. The same holds the other way round: A A⁻¹ = I. The picture multiplies a matrix by one that undoes it, and the product is I.

lead.text: A⁻¹ undoes whatever A does to a point.

reveal.text: Undoing A leaves every vector unchanged, which is what the identity matrix does.

lead.text: The 2 × 2 identity matrix leaves every vector as it was. Think about what undoing that would take.

reveal.text: You reasoned that undoing a map that does nothing needs no change. The identity is its own inverse.

lead.text: Some inverses can be found by thinking about what the matrix does. A matrix with entries only on its diagonal, such as rows (2, 0) and (0, 5), stretches the across values by 2 and the up values by 5. To undo a stretch you shrink by the same amount, so the inverse has the reciprocals on its diagonal: rows (1/2, 0) and (0, 1/5). A negative entry such as −4 flips the direction, and its reciprocal −1/4 flips it back.

A slide is the second kind. The matrix with rows (1, 3) and (0, 1) moves each point sideways by three times its up value, and a map of this kind is called a shear. To undo it, slide back by the same amount, which is the matrix with rows (1, −3) and (0, 1).
These two cases work entry by entry. A general matrix mixes the across and up values together, so it needs a recipe. The next screens build one.
The matrix A has rows (1, 2) and (0, 1). It slides each point sideways by twice its up value.

reveal.text: You slid back by the same amount, so the entry changes sign. The inverse of a shear is the shear in the opposite direction.

lead.text: A general matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d) mixes the across and up values, so its inverse needs more than reciprocals. There is a short recipe. First work out the number ad − bc, which is a times d minus b times c. Next swap a and d and change the signs of b and c. Finally divide every entry by ad − bc.

Try it on the matrix with rows (4, 1) and (7, 2). Here ad − bc = 4 × 2 − 1 × 7 = 1, so the inverse has rows (2, −1) and (−7, 4). Multiplying confirms it: row 1 of A dotted with column 1 of the inverse is 4 × 2 + 1 × (−7) = 1, and the other three entries come out as 0, 0 and 1.
The division is the weak point. If ad − bc is 0 the recipe asks you to divide by zero, so there is no inverse.

workedSteps.text: Find ad − bc, from the entries a = 3, b = 1, c = 5 and d = 2.
Swap the diagonal entries and negate the other two, then divide by ad − bc.
If ad − bc were zero, this division would fail and there would be no inverse.

steps.headline: Find entry (2, 2) of the inverse of A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Find ad − bc.
Swap the diagonal entries and negate the other two, then divide by that number. What is entry (2, 2) of the inverse?

lead.text: Return to the number ad − bc and see what it means when it is 0. Take the matrix with rows (1, 3) and (2, 6), where 1 × 6 − 3 × 2 = 0. It sends (3, 0) to (3, 6), and it sends (0, 1) to (3, 6) as well. Two different inputs land on the same output.

An inverse has to take each output back to one input, and this output came from two. No machine can know which one to return, so there is no inverse. The matrix has pushed every point onto a single line, and the information about where each point started is gone.
So a 2 × 2 matrix has an inverse exactly when ad − bc is not 0. The test takes one subtraction and settles the question before any other work.

Here is why inverses matter. Suppose a machine with matrix A produced the output b, and you want the input v. The machine's work is A v = b. Apply A⁻¹ to both sides and the left side becomes A⁻¹ A v = I v = v, so v = A⁻¹ b.

Take A with rows (3, 1) and (5, 2), whose inverse has rows (2, −1) and (−5, 3). If the output was (5, 9), the input is the inverse dotted with it: 2 × 5 − 1 × 9 = 1 across and −5 × 5 + 3 × 9 = 2 up. So the hidden input was (1, 2), and A(1, 2) = (3 + 2, 5 + 4) = (5, 9) confirms it.
An inverse turns the question of what went in into a multiplication, and it works for any machine that can be undone.
A machine with matrix A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ turned a hidden input v into the output (1, −2). Undo the machine to recover v.

blocks.text: A machine doubles a number and then adds 3. You never see what went in. This time the machine gave back 17, and to find the input you have to work backwards, undoing each step.

Matrices on the plane raise the same problem. A machine has moved or stretched a point, and all you hold is where it landed. To get the original point back you need a second machine that reverses the first, one that leaves the plane exactly where it began.

This lesson looks at that reversing machine and at a matrix that does nothing at all. We find a recipe for undoing any 2 × 2 matrix that can be undone. We also meet matrices that cannot, because they lose information.

intro.promise: By the end you'll undo a matrix map, and spot a matrix whose work cannot be undone.

recap.keyIdea: An inverse undoes a map: A⁻¹ A = I, the matrix that does nothing. A 2 × 2 matrix has an inverse when ad − bc is not 0, and then A v = b is solved by v = A⁻¹ b.

blocks.text: Back at the machine that gave 17, undoing meant reversing the steps in the opposite order. You found that the identity is its own inverse and built the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix. You also recovered a hidden input.

recap.nextHook: Recovering an input with an inverse is one way to solve equations, and the formula gets heavy for larger systems. The next lesson solves them with a routine you can run by hand, row by row.

lessons.title: Solve by row reduction

lead.text: Equations that describe the same situation form a system of equations. Each equation is a fact about the unknowns, the quantities you are trying to find, and a solution is a set of values that makes every equation true at once.

Systems give way to one idea. Suppose a ticket and a snack cost £7 together, and a ticket with three snacks costs £13. The second purchase is the first plus two more snacks, and it costs £6 more. So two snacks cost £6 and one snack costs £3. That makes the ticket £4. Subtracting one equation from the other made the ticket drop out, leaving a fact about snacks alone.
That is the whole method in miniature. Combine the equations so that one unknown disappears, and solve for the one that remains. Then put its value back into an equation to find the other.
Compare the two purchases and see what the extra item costs.

reveal.text: The second purchase has one more pencil and costs £2 more, so a pencil costs £2.

lead.text: Subtraction removes an unknown when its amounts match in both equations. Sometimes the amounts are opposites instead. Name the unknowns x₁ and x₂ so that equations are quicker to write, and take x₁ + x₂ = 7 and x₁ − x₂ = 1.

Both equations are true at once, so adding their sides is legitimate: equal things added to equal things stay equal. The x₂ terms cancel, so the left sides add to 2x₁ and the right sides add to 8. That gives 2x₁ = 8 and x₁ = 4. Put that into the first equation: 4 + x₂ = 7, so x₂ = 3.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows a system of this kind. Add the two rows in your head and see which unknown cancels. Adding and subtracting are the same kind of move, because both combine whole equations.

lead.text: Two equations: x₁ + x₂ = 5 and 2x₁ − x₂ = 1. Adding two true equations gives another true equation.

reveal.text: You added the equations so that x₂ cancelled. Row operations do the same job in an organised way.

steps.headline: Writing a system as a matrix

lead.text: Writing every x₁ and x₂ gets heavy as systems grow. The names of the unknowns carry no information, so we can drop them and keep only the numbers. The system 2x₁ + x₂ = 5 and x₁ + x₂ = 3 becomes a matrix with a row for each equation, with the right-hand sides added as a last column. This is called an augmented matrix.

Combining equations now becomes work on rows, and each move is a row operation. Three kinds never change the solution. One is to swap two rows. Another is to scale a row by a nonzero number. The third is to add a multiple of one row to another. Each one acts on the whole row, the right-hand number included, because a row is a whole equation.

Take row 2 from row 1, which is written R₁ ← R₁ − R₂ and means replace row 1 by row 1 minus row 2. Row 1 becomes (1, 0, 2), which says x₁ = 2. Put that into the second equation: 2 + x₂ = 3, so x₂ = 1.
Row operations act on whole equations and keep every solution.

reveal.text: Adding a multiple of one row to another is allowed. It keeps every solution.

lead.text: The subtraction above worked because the first column held matching entries. In general you create the zero yourself. Take x₁ + x₂ = 4 and 2x₁ + 3x₂ = 11, with augmented matrix rows (1, 1, 4) and (2, 3, 11). To get a zero under the leading 1, subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2: R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁.

Do it entry by entry, right-hand side included. The first entry is 2 − 2 × 1 = 0. The second is 3 − 2 × 1 = 1, and the last is 11 − 2 × 4 = 3. The new second row (0, 1, 3) has only one unknown left, and it says x₂ = 3.

Now go back up. Put x₂ = 3 into row 1: x₁ + 3 = 4, so x₁ = 1. Solving the bottom row first and carrying each answer into the rows above is called back-substitution. Check the result in the original equations: 1 + 3 = 4 and 2 × 1 + 3 × 3 = 11.

workedSteps.text: Write the augmented matrix.
Subtract 3 × row 1 from row 2. Do it to the right-hand side too.
Row 2 says −x₂ = −3, so x₂ = 3. Put that in row 1: x₁ + 6 = 7.

steps.headline: Start from x₁ + x₂ = 5 and 2x₁ − x₂ = 1. Perform R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁.

workedSteps.text: Subtract twice row 1 from row 2, entry by entry. The first entry becomes 2 − 2 = 0.
Now the right-hand side. What is the new right side of row 2?

lead.text: After reducing, the second equation is −3x₂ = −9 and the first is x₁ + x₂ = 5. Solve the row with a single unknown.

reveal.text: You solved the simple row first. That is back-substitution: work up from the row with one unknown.

lead.text: The routine scales up. With three unknowns each row has four numbers, and the aim is a staircase. The top row may hold all three unknowns, the next row holds two, and the last row holds one. A reduced system might read x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 9 on top, with x₂ + x₃ = 5 under it and x₃ = 2 at the bottom.
Start at the bottom, which already gives x₃ = 2. The middle row says x₂ + 2 = 5, so x₂ = 3. The top row says x₁ + 3 + 2 = 9, so x₁ = 4. Each solved unknown goes into the row above it.

Reaching the staircase takes row operations column by column: clear the entries under the first unknown, and then those under the second. Rows can also be swapped. If the equation you want at the top is missing, swap rows to bring it up.
Sometimes the first equation has no x₁ in it. Rows can be swapped, so start with whichever equation is simplest.

blocks.text: A pen and a pencil cost £5 together. A pen and two pencils cost £7. Nobody has told you either price, yet the two facts are enough to find both. You can even see how to start: the second purchase is the first with one pencil added.

The last lesson recovered a hidden input by undoing a matrix, which works well for two unknowns and gets heavy when there are more. Here we use the trick you can see in the pen and pencil prices, comparing one fact with another until an unknown drops out. Then we turn it into a routine that fits in a small table of numbers.
By the end you'll have a method that solves any small set of equations by hand, and a way to check the answer.

intro.promise: By the end you'll solve a pair of equations by row operations, then check your answer.

recap.keyIdea: Row operations keep a system's solution while simplifying it. Reduce until one unknown stands alone in a row, then back-substitute to find the rest.

blocks.text: Back at the pens and pencils, you made an unknown vanish by combining equations and then wrote the system as an augmented matrix. You found that R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁ leaves −9 on the right.

recap.nextHook: The routine finished neatly every time here, but a system can end in a row that makes no sense, or in a row of zeros. The next lesson reads what those rows say about how many solutions a system has.

lessons.title: One, none or many solutions

lead.text: Each equation in two unknowns picks out a line of points on a sheet of graph paper. The equation x + y = 3 holds for (3, 0), (2, 1) and (0, 3), and for every point between and beyond them, all of which lie on one straight line. A solution of two equations is a point that lies on both lines.

Two straight lines can meet in three ways. They can cross at a single point, so there is exactly one solution: x + y = 3 and x − y = 1 cross at (2, 1). They can run side by side and never meet, so there is no solution: x + y = 3 and x + y = 5 cannot both hold, since x + y cannot be 3 and 5 together. Or they can lie on top of each other, so every point of the line is a solution: x + y = 2 and 3x + 3y = 6 are the same line, because dividing the second by 3 gives the first.
Every pair of equations falls into one of these three cases, and the numbers will tell us which.
Divide the second statement by 2 and compare it with the first.

reveal.text: Halving the second statement gives x + y = 4.5, a line that runs beside x + y = 4 and never meets it. No pair satisfies both.

lead.text: Row reduction shows the same cases in the numbers. Start with x₁ + 3x₂ = 2 and 2x₁ + 6x₂ = 7, and write the augmented matrix with rows (1, 3, 2) and (2, 6, 7). Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2.

The second row becomes (0, 0, 3), because 2 − 2 × 1 = 0, 6 − 2 × 3 = 0 and 7 − 2 × 2 = 3. Read it as an equation: 0x₁ + 0x₂ = 3, which says 0 = 3. No values of the unknowns make that true, and every solution has to satisfy every row. So the system has no solution, which is the case of two lines that never meet.
A row like this is the signal to stop. Whatever the other rows say, no solution exists. The same reading holds for 0 = 5, or for 0 equal to any nonzero number.
Read the row as an equation and ask whether any values of the unknowns could satisfy it.

reveal.text: A row that reads zero equals a nonzero number cannot be satisfied, so there is no solution.

lead.text: Now change the right-hand side. Take x₁ + 2x₂ = 4 and 2x₁ + 4x₂ = 8. Subtracting 2 times row 1 from row 2 turns the second row into (0, 0, 0), because 8 − 2 × 4 = 0 as well. The row reads 0 = 0, which is always true and tells us nothing new. The second equation was a double of the first, so it added no information.

That leaves one real equation, x₁ + 2x₂ = 4, for two unknowns. Choose any value for x₂ and x₁ follows. Choose x₂ = 0 and x₁ = 4, or choose x₂ = 1 and x₁ = 2. Every such pair satisfies both original equations, and the choices never run out.

Here x₂ can be anything, so it is called a free variable. A system with at least one solution is called consistent, and a consistent system with a free variable has infinitely many solutions. This is the case of two lines lying on top of each other.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 2 × row 1 from row 2. The second row becomes all zeros.
The zero row says 0 = 0, which is always true. How many solutions does the system have?

lead.text: The third case is the one you met in the last lesson. After reduction, each unknown has a row that pins it down. Take rows (1, 0, 4) and (0, 1, 1). They read x₁ = 4 and x₂ = 1, so there is exactly one solution.

The first nonzero entry of a row in a reduced matrix is called its pivot, and here the pivots are the two 1s. An unknown whose column holds a pivot is pinned by its row. A column with no pivot has no row to pin it, and that unknown is free, as x₂ was in the last example.

afterFigure.text: To read any system, look at the reduced rows. A row reading 0 = a nonzero number means no solution. Otherwise, if every column has a pivot there is one solution, and if some column has none there are infinitely many.

lead.text: Here the equations name both unknowns outright: x₁ = 2 and x₂ = 3.

reveal.text: You saw that each unknown is fixed by its own equation. Nothing is left free and nothing contradicts, so there is exactly one solution.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 2 × row 1 from row 2.
The second row says 0 = 1.
No values of x₁ and x₂ can satisfy it. The system has no solution.

lead.text: Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2, and read what the second row says.

reveal.text: You compared the two equations and found them in conflict. After reduction that conflict is a row reading 0 = a nonzero number.

lead.text: Free variables can be counted. A reduced system has some number of unknowns and some number of pivots, and each pivot pins one unknown. Whatever is left over is free, so a consistent system has (unknowns − pivots) free variables.

Take four unknowns with x₁ + x₂ + x₄ = 6 and x₃ + x₄ = 2. The pivots are in columns 1 and 3, so x₂ and x₄ are free: 4 − 2 = 2. Choose x₂ = s and x₄ = t, and the rest follow: x₃ = 2 − t and x₁ = 6 − s − t. Every choice of s and t gives a solution.
When there are no free variables, a consistent system has exactly one solution. Each free variable adds a direction in which you can move without breaking any equation.

One family of systems always has an answer. When every right-hand side is 0, the system is written A x = 0. Put x = 0 in and every row becomes a sum of products with zero, so every row gives 0. The zero vector solves every such system, and none of them can have no solution.

The question is whether there are others. Take x₁ − x₂ = 0 and x₂ − x₃ = 0, which have pivots in columns 1 and 2, so x₃ is free. Choose x₃ = t, and then x₂ = t and x₁ = t. Every solution has all three values equal: (0, 0, 0), (1, 1, 1), (2, 2, 2) and so on.
Three unknowns less two pivots leaves one free variable, so this system has infinitely many solutions. A system A x = 0 has either the zero vector alone as its solution or infinitely many.
A shop's three prices satisfy x₁ + x₃ = 3 and x₂ + 2x₃ = 4. The system is consistent.

blocks.text: I'm thinking of two numbers, x and y. I tell you that x + y = 4, and then I tell you that 2x + 2y = 9. You can try to find them, but something is odd. The second statement looks like a double of the first, and doubling 4 does not give 9.

Until now every system had exactly one answer, and the row-reduction routine always ended with each unknown pinned down. Some systems end differently. Some have no answer at all, as this one seems to have, and some have so many answers that you can never list them all.
This lesson learns to read the last rows of a reduced system and say which case you are in. We start with a picture of two lines on a sheet of paper, and then see the same three cases in the numbers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell from the reduced rows whether a system has one solution, none or infinitely many.

recap.keyIdea: After row reduction, a row reading 0 = a nonzero number means no solution. A consistent system with a free variable has infinitely many, and with none it has exactly one.

blocks.text: Back at the two statements about x and y, the second was a double of the first with the wrong right-hand side, so no pair satisfied both. You saw that two lines can cross, miss or coincide, and that free variables are the unknowns without a pivot.

recap.nextHook: The free variables of a system describe a shape, such as a line or a plane of solutions. The next lesson names that shape and asks which sets of vectors can be built from a few of them.

lessons.title: Spans and subspaces

lead.text: Start with the one-button remote. Each press moves the robot by the vector (1, 2), which is one tile across and two up. Two presses take it to (2, 4), three to (3, 6), and one press of the backwards button takes it to (−1, −2). Every place it can reach is the move multiplied by some number c, so every reachable place has the form c(1, 2).

Plot those places and they fall on one straight line that runs through the starting tile in both directions. A tile off that line, such as (1, 3), can never be reached with this remote. The set of everything the robot can reach has a name: it is the span of the vector (1, 2). More generally, the span of some vectors is every vector you can build from them by scaling and adding.

afterFigure.text: With one button the span is a line, and the figure shows two examples. A line gives the robot a single direction to travel in, which it can follow either way. To leave the line the robot needs a second button, which is where we go next.

lead.text: The remote has only the (1, 2) button and its backwards twin. The robot has stopped at a place whose across coordinate is 3.

reveal.text: Three presses reach (3, 6). Every reachable place is a multiple of (1, 2), so the up coordinate is always double the across coordinate.

lead.text: Now give the remote a second button that moves the robot by (1, 0), one tile across and none up. The robot can press both buttons in any mix. Press the first button twice and the second three times, and it ends at 2(1, 2) + 3(1, 0) = (2, 4) + (3, 0) = (5, 4). A total of that kind, with each move scaled by a number and the results added, is a combination of the two moves.

The span of the two moves is the set of all their combinations, and here it is the whole floor. The up coordinate of any combination comes only from the first button, so it settles how many presses that button needs. The second button then makes up whatever is missing across. Every tile can be reached this way.

afterFigure.text: Not every second button helps. Give the robot (2, 4) as its second move and it already had that: two presses of the first button make it. The new button adds no new direction, and the span stays the same line. The number of independent directions in a span is its dimension, so a line has dimension 1 and the whole floor has dimension 2. Two moves reach dimension 2 only when neither is a scaled copy of the other, and a scaled copy can point backwards, as (−1, −2) does.

lead.text: The remote has the buttons (1, 2) and (2, 4), each with a backwards twin.

reveal.text: You checked whether the second button adds a direction. A scaled copy gives nothing new, so the span stays a line.

lead.text: Now run the question backwards. The remote has the buttons (1, 0) and (1, 1), and the robot stands at (4, 1). How many presses of each button put it there? Call the two numbers c₁ and c₂, so that (4, 1) = c₁(1, 0) + c₂(1, 1). These numbers are the coefficients of the combination.

One vector equation hides one ordinary equation for each coordinate, and one of the two is easy. Look at the up coordinates. The button (1, 0) has no up part, so all of the up distance, 1, must come from the second button, and c₂ = 1. The across coordinates then say c₁ + c₂ = 4, and since c₂ is now known, c₁ = 3.

Check it by pressing: 3(1, 0) + 1(1, 1) = (3, 0) + (1, 1) = (4, 1). The habit to take away is to match one coordinate at a time, starting with the coordinate where only one button contributes. If no coefficients work, the target lies outside the span.

Match the first coordinates: c₁ + c₂ = 7.

steps.headline: A set that stays inside itself

lead.text: Every span we have met has one property worth noticing. Take the line through (1, 2) and pick two places on it, (2, 4) and (−1, −2). Their sum is (1, 2), which is on the line again. Scale (2, 4) by 5 and you get (10, 20), which is also on the line. Whichever way you add places on the line or scale them, the robot never leaves it.

A set of vectors with that behaviour is called a subspace. It has to contain the zero vector, and it has to stay inside itself, so that adding two members or scaling one always gives another member. The zero vector belongs because scaling any member by 0 produces it: a robot that presses nothing stays on its starting tile.

afterFigure.text: Every span is a subspace, because a sum of combinations of the same moves is another combination of them, and so is a scaled one. The line and the whole floor are both examples. The zero vector also gives a quick way to rule a set out: if a set misses it, the set cannot be a subspace.

steps.headline: A line that misses the start

lead.text: A straight line is not always a subspace. Take the points (x, y) with y = x + 3, a line that runs parallel to the diagonal through the starting tile but sits three units higher. The zero vector would need 0 = 0 + 3, which fails, so the starting tile is not on this line and the first requirement is broken.

The second requirement breaks too. The points (0, 3) and (1, 4) are both on the line, since 3 = 0 + 3 and 4 = 1 + 3. Their sum is (1, 7), and 7 is not 1 + 3 = 4, so adding two members has left the set.
The test has two parts. First ask whether the zero vector is in the set. If it is, ask whether adding and scaling keep you inside. The first question often settles the matter alone, as it does here.
Consider the line made of all points whose up distance is double their across distance.

reveal.text: That line is the span of (1, 2), so it contains the zero vector and stays inside itself under adding and scaling.

lead.text: A delivery drone is allowed to fly only along one straight path, and its pilot wants to treat the path as a space of its own.

blocks.text: The last lesson ended with solutions that fill out a line or a plane, whatever the number of unknowns. Those shapes turn up all through linear algebra, and a toy robot is a good way to meet them.

Picture the robot on a huge floor of square tiles, with you holding its remote. The remote has a single button. Each press moves the robot one tile across and two tiles up, and a second button runs the same move backwards. You mark the tile it starts on, and you can press as often as you like.

Some tiles are within reach and most are not. This lesson looks at the whole set of reachable tiles, at how it grows as the remote gets more buttons, and at which collections of tiles are tidy enough to count as a space of their own.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the dimension of a span and test whether a set is a subspace.

recap.keyIdea: A span is every combination of some vectors, and its dimension counts the independent directions. A subspace contains zero and stays inside itself under adding and scaling.

blocks.text: Back at the robot's remote, you saw that one button keeps it on a line and a second, different button frees it across the floor. You wrote (4, 1), (7, 4) and (5, 3) as combinations of two moves, and you ruled out a path that misses the starting tile.

recap.nextHook: Some remotes carry a button the robot never needed, such as (2, 4) beside (1, 2). The next lesson asks how few buttons still reach everywhere, and what that number says about the space.

lessons.title: Basis and dimension

lead.text: Look at the three buttons again: right (1, 0), up (0, 1) and diagonal (1, 1). The diagonal press does exactly what a right press followed by an up press does, since (1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1). Anything the robot can do with the diagonal button it could do without it, so that button adds nothing to the floor the robot can reach.

Vectors are called linearly independent when none of them can be made from the others. Right and up are independent, because no amount of pressing right will move the robot up, and no amount of pressing up will move it across. Each gives a direction that the other cannot. With the diagonal button added, the set stops being independent.

afterFigure.text: So the three buttons carry one spare. Remove the diagonal and the robot still reaches everywhere. Remove right instead and the robot can still manage with up and diagonal, because right is the diagonal minus the up. Any one of the three could go, but only one of them.

lead.text: The remote has the buttons right, up and diagonal. Taking buttons away can only shrink what the robot reaches.

reveal.text: Removing the diagonal leaves right and up, which still reach every tile. Removing a second button would leave a single line.

steps.headline: The smallest set that still reaches everywhere

lead.text: A set of vectors that is independent and spans a space is called a basis of that space. It is the smallest set that still reaches everything, because it has no spare vectors, and it is a complete set, because nothing is out of reach. Right and up form a basis of the floor.

A space has many bases. The pair (1, 1) and (1, −1) also reaches every tile: for instance (2, 0) = (1, 1) + (1, −1). These buttons point diagonally rather than along the grid, but the robot is just as free. They have something else in common with right and up, which is that there are two of them. One vector alone spans only a line, and with three vectors one is always spare.

afterFigure.text: That is true of every basis of the floor, with no exceptions. The number of vectors in a basis is the dimension of the space, and for the floor it is 2. This matches the earlier use of the word, since a span of dimension 2 is a plane.

lead.text: Think of any remote that reaches the whole floor with no spare button.

reveal.text: You matched the size of a basis to the dimension of the space. Every basis of the plane has the same size.

lead.text: A basis does more than reach everywhere. It gives each place exactly one recipe of presses. With only right and up, the tile (3, 2) needs exactly 3 presses of right and 2 of up. Those two numbers are the coordinates of the tile in that basis.

A remote with a spare button breaks this. With right, up and diagonal, the tile (3, 2) can be reached as 3 right and 2 up, or as 1 right and 2 diagonal, since (1, 0) + 2(1, 1) = (3, 2). That is two recipes, and there are infinitely many more, because the spare button can be traded against the others.

Two properties explain the contrast. Spanning guarantees that at least one recipe exists, and independence guarantees that there is at most one. A basis has both, so every vector has exactly one set of coordinates.

To find coordinates in another basis, match coordinates as in the last lesson. For the basis (1, 1) and (1, −1) and the tile (5, 1), the equations are c₁ + c₂ = 5 and c₁ − c₂ = 1. Adding them cancels c₂ and gives 2c₁ = 6, so c₁ = 3 and c₂ = 2.

Add the equations. The c₂ terms cancel.
Put c₁ back into the first equation.

Add the two equations. What is c₁?

lead.text: The basis is (1, 1) and (2, 0), and the target is (7, 3). Match the second coordinates first.

reveal.text: You found the up coordinate first, then used it for the across coordinate. A basis gave a single answer for each coefficient.

steps.headline: Counting the vectors in a basis

lead.text: Dimension is a count, and counting works for any space. A line has dimension 1, since one nonzero vector spans it. The floor has dimension 2. Ordinary space has dimension 3, because reaching every point of a room takes one button for each of three directions, and no basis of space has more or fewer.

The same count tells you how much a set of vectors really offers. The vectors (4, 1) and (1, 3) are independent, since neither is a multiple of the other, so their span has dimension 2. They form a basis of the floor even though they look nothing like right and up. The vectors (1, 2) and (2, 4) are a different story. Their span is a line, so the dimension is 1 and only one of them is doing any work.
In general, the dimension of a span is the number of vectors that remain when every spare has been removed.

One kind of spare is easy to miss. A button that moves the robot by (0, 0) does nothing at all, no matter how many times it is pressed. It is a combination of any other buttons, because it equals 0 times each of them. So a set that contains the zero vector is never independent, whatever else is in it.

The pair (3, 1) and (0, 0) shows what this costs. It holds two vectors, but it spans only the line through (3, 1), so its dimension is 1. A count of vectors overstates the dimension whenever a spare is hiding in the list.

To decide whether two vectors form a basis of the floor, ask whether either is zero or a scaled copy of the other. If so, they fail. If they point in different directions, they pass. A list of any other length fails at once, because a basis of the floor has exactly two.
A navigation app wants the fewest direction vectors that still reach everywhere. One candidate pair includes the zero vector.
