blocks.text: The last lesson showed that a remote can carry a button the robot never needed. Pressing (1, 2) twice does everything a separate (2, 4) button would, so the extra one is dead weight. That raises a design problem for a robot with three buttons.

Suppose the buttons move it right by (1, 0), up by (0, 1) and diagonally by (1, 1). Used forwards and backwards, they reach every tile of the floor. Each button costs money and adds another place for the remote to break, so you would like to keep as few as possible without losing any of the floor.

This lesson finds the smallest set of buttons that still reaches everywhere, shows that each place then has exactly one recipe of presses, and finds that the size of that smallest set never depends on which buttons you keep.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say whether vectors form a basis, and find the coordinates of a vector in a given basis.

recap.keyIdea: A basis spans a space with no redundancy, and every basis of it has the same size: its dimension. Each vector then has exactly one set of coordinates.

blocks.text: Back at the remote, you trimmed three buttons to two and saw that every place then has just one recipe. In the basis (1, 1), (1, −1) you wrote (4, 2) with c₁ = 3, and you found that a button that does nothing is never needed.

recap.nextHook: So far the remote has set where the robot can go. The next lesson hands the robot a machine instead, a matrix, and asks how many independent directions come out of it and which inputs it sends to nothing.

lessons.title: Rank and null space

lead.text: Return to the sum machine. It turns (x, y) into x + y, which is what the matrix with the single row (1, 1) does to its input. An input comes out as zero exactly when x + y = 0. So (2, −2) vanishes, and so do (5, −5) and (0, 0), and so does every point of the form (t, −t). Plotted, they make a line through the origin.

The set of all inputs that a matrix sends to zero is its null space. The zero vector is always in it, since a matrix applied to nothing gives nothing. Here the null space is a whole line, so the machine throws away a direction: moving along that line changes nothing about the output. The null space is a subspace, because the sum of two inputs that vanish also vanishes, and so does any multiple of one.
That is why the null space matters. Two inputs that differ by a vector in it give the same output, so it measures how much the machine loses.
The sum machine adds the two coordinates of its input. This time the input has x = 5.

reveal.text: 5 + y = 0 gives y = −5. The point (5, −5) lies on the null-space line y = −x.

lead.text: Now look at the other end of the machine. Take the matrix B with rows (1, 0, 2) and (0, 1, 3). It takes three numbers in and gives two out: B(x, y, z) = (x + 2z, y + 3z). Split the input into its parts and the output becomes x(1, 0) + y(0, 1) + z(2, 3). Whatever you put in, the output is a combination of the columns of B.

So the set of all outputs is the span of the columns, and it is called the column space. For B the first two columns, (1, 0) and (0, 1), already span the whole plane, so the column space is the plane. The third column (2, 3) is a combination of the first two, so it adds no new output.

afterFigure.text: The dimension of the column space is called the rank of the matrix. B has rank 2: of its three columns, only two give independent directions. The rank counts the variety of outputs in the way that the dimension of a span counted the directions of the robot.

lead.text: Apply A, with rows (1, 2, 0) and (0, 0, 1), to the input (−2, 1, 0). Dot the first row with the input to get the first coordinate of the output.

reveal.text: The first row gives −2 + 2 + 0 = 0, and the second row gives 0. The whole output is zero, so this input is in the null space of A.

lead.text: The rank can be found without drawing anything. Reduce the matrix with row operations, as in the earlier lessons. Then count the pivots. Each pivot marks a column that brings a new direction, and a column without a pivot is a combination of the columns before it. B is already reduced: it has pivots in columns 1 and 2, so its rank is 2.

A matrix with many columns can still have a small rank. If the second row of a matrix is twice its first row, reduction turns the second row into zeros, which leaves one pivot at most and rank 1. The rank can never exceed the number of rows or the number of columns, because each pivot needs a row and a column of its own.

Columns with a pivot give outputs. The columns without one are the free columns, like the free variables of the earlier lessons, and each of them lets the input change without changing the output. For B the third column has no pivot, so z is free. Set z = 1 and solve B(x, y, 1) = (0, 0): then x = −2 and y = −3. So (−2, −3, 1) is in the null space, and so is every multiple of it.
The dimension of the null space is called the nullity, and it equals the number of free columns. Every column either has a pivot or does not, so the two counts add up to the number of columns.
For B that is 2 + 1 = 3. The sum gives a matrix a fixed budget of columns. Each column either contributes a new output direction or is a direction that the machine throws away.

steps.headline: Find the rank and nullity of $\begin{pmatrix}1&3&0&2\\0&0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: The matrix is already reduced. There are pivots in columns 1 and 3.
The matrix has 4 columns. The nullity is the columns that are left over.
Row 1 has its first nonzero entry in column 1. Row 2 has its first nonzero entry in column 3.
Count the pivots. What is the rank?

lead.text: The matrix A has rows (1, 2, 0) and (0, 0, 1), so it has three columns. You know its rank.

reveal.text: You took the rank away from the number of columns. Each column without a pivot is a free direction, and those directions are the null space.

lead.text: The column space is built from the columns of the original matrix, so a basis for it must be made of those columns. Take E with rows (0, 1, 2) and (0, 2, 5). Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2 and the rows become (0, 1, 2) and (0, 0, 1). The pivots are in columns 2 and 3.

Those are the columns to keep, but read them from E, because row operations change the columns and only the positions of the pivots carry over. The original columns 2 and 3 are (1, 2) and (2, 5). They are independent, and there are as many of them as the rank, so they form a basis of the column space. Column 1 is the zero vector, which adds nothing.
To pick a basis for the column space, row-reduce to find where the pivots are. Then take the columns in those positions from the original matrix.
A designer must pick, from the three columns of A, the fewest that still give every output.

blocks.text: The last lesson counted the buttons a robot really needs. This lesson gives the robot a machine instead of a remote, and looks at what the machine does to whatever you put into it.

Here is the smallest machine we can build. You feed it a point (x, y) and it hands back one number, the sum x + y. Feed it (3, 1) and it returns 4. Feed it (2, −2) and it returns 0. Many different points give the same answer, and a whole line of them give the answer 0, because every pair with y = −x adds up to nothing.

A matrix is a machine of this kind, and two things are worth knowing about any matrix. One is which inputs it sends to zero. The other is how much variety can come out of it. This lesson counts both and finds that the two counts are linked.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count a matrix's rank and nullity, and say which inputs it sends to zero.

recap.keyIdea: The rank counts the independent output directions and the nullity counts the inputs sent to zero. Together they add up to the number of columns.

blocks.text: Back at the sum machine, you found that the inputs it sends to zero form a line. For the three-column matrix A you counted rank 2 and nullity 1, checked that (−2, 1, 0) is sent to zero, and chose columns 1 and 3 as a basis.

recap.nextHook: A matrix can also stretch the floor it acts on, and when it squashes everything onto a line it has lost a dimension for good. The next lesson measures how much a matrix stretches area, and what the number says when the area vanishes.

lessons.title: Determinants and volume

lead.text: Start with the simple case from the rubber sheet. A matrix with entries a and d on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere stretches by a across and by d up. The corners (1, 0) and (0, 1) of the tile go to (a, 0) and (0, d), so the 1 m square becomes a rectangle a metres across and d metres up. Its area is a × d.

Every other square on the sheet is stretched the same way, so every area is multiplied by a × d, not only the tile's. A region of 4 m² becomes 4 × a × d. That makes a × d the area factor of the map, the one number that says how many times larger any area becomes.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows a map that stretches by 3 across and 4 up. It turns the tile into a rectangle of area 12, so its area factor is 12. The diagonal case is the easy one. For a general matrix the tile does not stay a rectangle, so the next step is to see what shape it becomes and how to measure it.

lead.text: A map stretches every length across by 5 and every length up by 2. It sends a square tile of side 1 m to a rectangle.

reveal.text: The sides become 5 m and 2 m, so the area is 5 × 2 = 10 m². Stretches in separate directions multiply.

lead.text: A general 2 × 2 matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d) sends the corner (1, 0) of the tile to (a, c), its first column, and the corner (0, 1) to (b, d), its second column. The square becomes a parallelogram whose sides are those two columns. Take the rows (3, 1) and (2, 2), whose columns are (3, 2) and (1, 2).

Fit the parallelogram inside a rectangle with sides along the axes. Its far corner is (3 + 1, 2 + 2) = (4, 4), so the rectangle is 4 by 4 with area 16. Four kinds of piece lie outside the parallelogram. Two triangles each have area 3 × 2 ÷ 2 = 3, which makes 6. Two more have area 1 × 2 ÷ 2 = 1 each, which makes 2. Two small rectangles are 1 by 2, which makes 4. The parallelogram has area 16 − 6 − 2 − 4 = 4.

afterFigure.text: Doing the same sums with letters in place of numbers leaves ad − bc, which here is 3 × 2 − 1 × 2 = 4. This number is the determinant of the matrix. Take the product of the main diagonal and subtract the product of the other diagonal. When b and c are zero it shrinks to the a × d of the diagonal case.

lead.text: The determinant can be negative. Swap the two rows of the matrix above and its rows become (2, 2) and (3, 1), with determinant 2 × 1 − 2 × 3 = −4. The tile still becomes a parallelogram of area 4, but turned over, as if the rubber sheet had been flipped. The sign records whether the map keeps the tile the right way round or turns it over. The area factor is the size of the determinant with the sign dropped.

Zero is the other special value. Take rows (1, 3) and (2, 6). The second row is double the first. The columns (1, 2) and (3, 6) lie along one line, so the parallelogram has no width. The determinant is 1 × 6 − 3 × 2 = 0, which is the area of a flat shape.
A determinant of zero means the map flattens the whole floor onto a line. Different points then land on the same spot and nothing can send them back, so a map with determinant 0 has no inverse.
The matrix with rows (−2, 0) and (0, 3) flips the direction across and stretches by 2 there. Up it stretches by 3.

reveal.text: You multiplied the two stretches and dropped the sign. The determinant is −6, and its size, 6, is the area factor.

workedSteps.text: Multiply the main diagonal.
Multiply the other diagonal.
Subtract. The area scales by 7, and the sign says the tile is turned over.
Main diagonal product.
Other diagonal product.
Subtract the second from the first. What is the determinant?

lead.text: Swap the two rows of the previous matrix to get rows (1, 3) and (2, 1). Then work out its determinant.

reveal.text: You found the same size with the opposite sign. Swapping rows turns the tile over, and the sign records it.

lead.text: Run a tile through one map and then through another. The first map multiplies its area by the first determinant, and the second map multiplies the result by its own determinant. The two maps together are the matrix product from the earlier lessons, so the product multiplies area by both factors: det(A B) = det A × det B.

Take A with rows (3, 0) and (0, 2), whose determinant is 6, and B with rows (1, 2) and (0, 3), whose determinant is 3. Their product A B has rows (3, 6) and (0, 6), and its determinant is 3 × 6 − 6 × 0 = 18, which is 6 × 3.

The rule also explains why a map with determinant 0 has no inverse. If an inverse existed, doing the map and then its inverse would be the identity, whose determinant is 1. A product with a zero in it cannot equal 1.

In space the same ideas hold with volume in place of area. A diagonal map scales each direction by its own factor, and a cube of side 1 m becomes a box with those three side lengths. Scales of 2 across, 5 up and 3 deep give a box 2 m by 5 m by 3 m, with volume 30 m³.

So a 3 × 3 matrix has a determinant too, and it is the factor for volume. For a diagonal matrix it is the product of the diagonal entries. The sign still records a turn-over, and a zero still means a collapse, now of space onto a plane or a line.
Everything for the 2 × 2 case carries over, though the formula for a general 3 × 3 matrix is longer. The idea stays the same: the determinant is the signed number by which a map multiplies size.
Work with a cube that is 1 m on each side.

blocks.text: The last lesson counted directions: how many independent outputs a matrix has. A matrix does more to the floor than keep or lose directions, because it also stretches it. A good way to see this is to draw a square tile, 1 m by 1 m, on a sheet of stretchy rubber and then pull the sheet.

Pull it three times as far across and five times as far up, and the square becomes a rectangle 3 m by 5 m. Its area has grown from 1 m² to 15 m². Drag one corner sideways instead and the square leans over into a slanted shape whose area is harder to guess. Turn the sheet over and the tile comes back mirror-reversed, with the same area.
This lesson finds one number for each matrix that says how much the map multiplies area by. The number carries a sign, and it turns out to be zero exactly when the map flattens the floor onto a line.

intro.promise: By the end you'll calculate a 2 × 2 determinant and read what it says about area.

recap.keyIdea: A determinant is the signed factor by which a map scales area or volume. Zero means the map collapses space, so there is no inverse.

blocks.text: Back at the rubber sheet, you found that a map multiplies area by its determinant. You calculated a determinant of 5, then −5 after swapping the rows. Dependent columns gave 0, and scale factors multiplied to 24 and 12.

recap.nextHook: Maps can also flatten the floor onto a line, and dropping a point straight onto a line is the simplest case of that. The next lesson finds exactly where a point lands and how much of it is left over.

lessons.title: Project onto a direction

lead.text: Take a point v = (8, 3) and the ground, which is the line along the x axis. Drop the point straight down. It lands at (8, 0), keeping its across position and losing its height. This landing place is called the projection of v onto the line. Dropping straight down is what makes the projection special, because of all the points on the ground, (8, 0) is the nearest to v.

A line through the origin can be described by a direction, a vector d that lies along it. The ground has direction (1, 0), and every point of the ground is a multiple of that direction. So the projection of v onto the ground is some multiple c of d, and our task is to find that number c. For the ground it can be read off the picture: c = 8.

afterFigure.text: The ground is a convenient case because the drop is vertical and we can see where it lands. The second case in the figure gives the same ground the direction (2, 0). The landing place does not move. A slanted line has no such shortcut, and the rest of the lesson builds a rule that works for any line.

lead.text: A point sits at (6, 5): 6 along the ground and 5 up. It is dropped straight down onto the ground line.

reveal.text: Dropping straight down keeps the across position and loses the height, so the point lands 6 along the ground.

lead.text: Now tilt the line. Let d = (1, 2), a ramp that rises two for every one across, and let v = (0, 5). Drop v straight onto the ramp, meaning that the piece joining v to its landing place makes a right angle with the ramp. Call that piece the residual. It is v minus the projection, the part of v that the line cannot account for.

The projection is c times d for some number c, so the residual is v − c d. A right angle means a dot product of zero, as in the lesson on orthogonal vectors, so (v − c d) · d = 0. Expanding gives v · d − c (d · d) = 0, which means c = (v · d) ÷ (d · d).

afterFigure.text: For this ramp v · d = 0 × 1 + 5 × 2 = 10 and d · d = 1 + 4 = 5, so c = 2. The projection is 2(1, 2) = (2, 4) and the residual is (0, 5) − (2, 4) = (−2, 1). Check the right angle: (−2, 1) · (1, 2) = −2 + 2 = 0. Writing the direction as (2, 4) instead gives the same landing place, because a longer d needs fewer copies.

lead.text: Use the rule from the last screen. Dot v with d, dot d with itself, then divide the first number by the second.

reveal.text: You found v · d = 8 and d · d = 2, so the coefficient is 4. The projection is 4 copies of d.

lead.text: Here is the recipe from start to finish. Dot v with d, and dot d with itself. Divide the first number by the second to get c, the number of copies of d you need. Scaling d by c gives the projection. Subtracting that from v gives the residual.

Two checks catch most slips. Scaling d changes c but never the projection, because a longer d needs fewer copies. And when v and d already make a right angle, v · d = 0, so c = 0 and the projection is the zero vector: the whole of v is residual.
The opposite case also happens. When v already lies along d, the projection is v itself and the residual is zero.

steps.headline: Project v = (5, 1) onto d = (1, 1), then find the residual.

workedSteps.text: Dot v with d, and d with itself.
The coefficient is 6 ÷ 2. Scale d by it.
Subtract the projection from v to get the residual.

steps.headline: Project (4, 2) onto the line spanned by (1, 1). Find the x coordinate.

workedSteps.text: Dot the vectors.
Scale d by the coefficient. What is the x coordinate of the projection?

lead.text: The vector is (−2, 4) and the direction is (1, 1). Follow the same recipe as before.

reveal.text: Your answer is a multiple of (1, 1). A projection always lies on the line it projects onto.

lead.text: The projection and the residual split v into two pieces. One lies along the line and the other lies across it at a right angle. Adding them gives v back. For v = (5, 1) and d = (1, 1) we had (3, 3) + (2, −2) = (5, 1).

Engineers split forces this way. A sailing boat feels a force of (7, 1) but can only move along the line (1, 1). Here v · d = 8 and d · d = 2, so c = 4 and the part along the line is (4, 4). The part across it is (7, 1) − (4, 4) = (3, −3), which makes a right angle with (1, 1) because 3 − 3 = 0. Only the along part drives the boat forward, and the keel absorbs the rest.

steps.headline: The nearest point on the line

lead.text: The projection is also the point of the line nearest to v. Take the projection q and any other point p on the line. The residual runs from q to v at a right angle to the line, and the piece of line from q to p lies along the line. These two sides meet at a right angle, so the distance from p to v is the long side of a right-angled triangle, and it is longer than the residual.

This is why the projection matters beyond tidy geometry. When an exact answer is out of reach, the closest answer that is reachable is a projection. A system with no solution has a target that sits off the span of its columns, and the best we can do is the nearest point of that span. That is the problem the next lesson solves.
A kite is pulled with force (4, 2). Along the rope's direction (1, 1) the pull is (3, 3). The sideways part is the residual: the force minus that pull.

blocks.text: A determinant of zero meant that a map flattens the floor onto a line, with many points landing on the same spot. This lesson looks at the simplest flattening, which is dropping a point straight onto a line, and works out where the point lands.

Picture a bird hovering over a flat field at noon, with the sun directly overhead. Its shadow is the spot on the ground directly below it. If the bird is 9 m along the field and 4 m up, the shadow is 9 m along the field. Nothing about the bird's position along the field has changed, and the 4 m of height is what the shadow leaves out.

The ground is easy because it is horizontal. This lesson handles a line at any slant, such as a ramp, by finding where a point lands on it and what is left over. It ends by showing that the landing place is the closest point of the line.

intro.promise: By the end you'll project a vector onto a direction, and find the perpendicular part that is left over.

recap.keyIdea: The projection of v onto d is ((v · d) ÷ (d · d)) d, the closest point on the line. The residual v − projection is perpendicular to d.

blocks.text: Back at the shadow on the field, you found that the same recipe works for any slant. You projected (4, 2) onto (1, 1) to get x = 3, saw that the residual is perpendicular to the line, and found that a perpendicular vector projects to zero.

recap.nextHook: Sometimes no exact answer exists, such as when a set of measurements disagree. The next lesson shows that the closest answer is also a projection, and uses it to pick the best fit.

lessons.title: Fit with least squares

lead.text: Call the bolt's true length x. Each reading is a claim about x: x = 6, x = 7 and x = 11. Written as columns, that is x times the column (1, 1, 1) on the left and the column of readings (6, 7, 11) on the right. The column of ones has three rows because there are three readings.

Now ask what a single x can produce on the left. Only multiples of (1, 1, 1), such as (3, 3, 3) or (8, 8, 8), where every entry is the same. In three-dimensional space that is a line through the origin, the span of one vector. The readings are not all equal, so they sit off that line and no value of x solves the equation.

afterFigure.text: The last lesson's idea applies here. Take the point of the line that is nearest to the readings, which is their projection onto the direction d = (1, 1, 1). The coefficient is (v · d) ÷ (d · d) = (6 + 7 + 11) ÷ 3 = 8. The nearest point is 8 copies of (1, 1, 1), so the best single value is 8 cm. That is the average of the readings, and projection shows why it is the right choice: no other value gives a point nearer to them.

lead.text: Another bolt reads 1 cm, 2 cm and 6 cm. Project the readings onto (1, 1, 1), as with the first bolt, to find the one value that fits them best.

reveal.text: You projected (1, 2, 6) onto (1, 1, 1). The coefficient is (1 + 2 + 6) ÷ 3 = 3, which is the average of the readings.

lead.text: Next, check how well 8 cm does by comparing each reading with it. The readings 6, 7 and 11 miss 8 by −2, −1 and 3. Each gap, a reading minus the fitted value, is a residual. It is the same residual as in the last lesson, the part of the readings that the fit leaves unexplained, and as a column it is (−2, −1, 3).

The residuals add up to zero. The last lesson showed that the residual of a projection is perpendicular to the direction, and here the direction is (1, 1, 1). Perpendicular means a dot product of zero, and the dot product of (−2, −1, 3) with (1, 1, 1) is just the sum of its entries. So the misses above the fit and the misses below it balance exactly.

To compare fits we need one number for the size of the misses. The plain sum cannot do it, because it cancels. So each residual is squared first and the squares are added. Squaring makes every miss positive and makes a big miss count for more. For the value 8 the total is 4 + 1 + 9 = 14. The middle reading, 7, leaves residuals −1, 0 and 4, and their squares add up to 17, which is worse.

The fit with the smallest total of squared residuals is called the least-squares fit. That total is the squared length of the residual column, and a projection is the nearest point there is. So the projection has the smallest total of all, and that is why 8 beats 7 and every other value.

steps.headline: Fit one constant to 2, 3 and 10, then total the squared residuals.

workedSteps.text: Project onto (1, 1, 1). The best constant is the average: 15 ÷ 3.
The residuals are measurement minus fit. They add up to zero.
Square each residual and add.

steps.headline: Measurements 2, 4 and 9 are fitted by the constant 5. Total the squared residuals.

workedSteps.text: The residuals are 2 − 5, 4 − 5 and 9 − 5.
Square each one and add. What is the total?

lead.text: The residuals of the fit 5 to the measurements 2, 4 and 9 are −3, −1 and 4. Add them as they are, with their signs.

reveal.text: You found they cancel. The residuals of a least-squares constant are perpendicular to (1, 1, 1), so they always sum to zero.

lead.text: A single constant suits readings that should all be the same. Often a quantity changes steadily, and then a line fits better. A seedling is measured at planting, in week 0, and again in weeks 1 and 2, and stands 3 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm tall. A line c + s x describes its height after x weeks: c is the starting height and s is the slope, the number of centimetres gained each week.

Each measurement is one equation. Week 0 gives c + 0s = 3, week 1 gives c + 1s = 3 and week 2 gives c + 2s = 6. As columns, that is c times (1, 1, 1) plus s times (0, 1, 2), set equal to the heights (3, 3, 6). The first column is the one from the bolt, and the second holds the weeks. With two unknowns the left side can make every mix of the two columns, which fills a flat sheet through the origin and is wider than a single line.

afterFigure.text: The heights (3, 3, 6) do not lie on a straight line, so they are off the sheet. The method is the one from the bolt, one dimension up. The best c and s give the point of the sheet nearest to the heights, and the residuals are perpendicular to both columns. Working it through gives c = 2.5 and s = 1.5. The fitted line 2.5 + 1.5x predicts 2.5, 4 and 5.5 cm, which miss the measurements by 0.5, −1 and 0.5.

lead.text: Solving for c and s from scratch is slow, but evenly spaced measurements allow a shortcut. Take measurements at x = 0, 1 and 2, and call the residuals r₀, r₁ and r₂. Perpendicular to the column (1, 1, 1) means r₀ + r₁ + r₂ = 0. Perpendicular to the column (0, 1, 2) means r₁ + 2r₂ = 0, because the first entry is multiplied by 0. The second equation gives r₁ = −2r₂, and putting that into the first leaves r₀ = r₂.

So the first and last residuals are equal. A residual is a measurement minus the line, and the line rises by 2s between x = 0 and x = 2, so equal residuals mean that the measurements rise by exactly 2s as well. In symbols, last y − first y = 2s, which gives s = (last y − first y) ÷ 2. For the seedling this is (6 − 3) ÷ 2 = 1.5, as the figure showed.

The middle measurement plays no part in the slope. It still matters for c, because the residuals sum to zero, which makes c the average of the measurements minus s. For the seedling that is 4 − 1.5 = 2.5. The shortcut works only for measurements at x = 0, 1 and 2.
A vine is measured in weeks 0, 1 and 2 and stands 5 cm, 9 cm and 7 cm tall. Use the shortcut to find the slope of the best line c + s x.

reveal.text: You used only the first and last measurements: (7 − 5) ÷ 2 = 1. The middle one, 9, moves c and leaves the slope alone.

lead.text: A taxi's fare is £2, £5 and £8 for trips of 0, 1 and 2 km. Fit a line c + s x through these fares, where s is the cost of each extra kilometre.

blocks.text: You are measuring a metal bolt with a cheap ruler. Three readings give 6 cm, 7 cm and 11 cm. The ruler is worn at one end, so the readings disagree and no single length can match all of them.

A report still needs one number. The middle reading, 7 cm, ignores the other two. The largest, 11 cm, trusts one glance over the rest. Averaging feels fair, yet a feeling is a weak reason for choosing it.

The last lesson ended with an idea that settles this. When no exact answer exists, the best answer is the nearest one that can be reached, and that is a projection. This lesson applies it to the bolt and makes the word nearest precise. After that it fits a straight line through points that do not quite line up.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the best constant or straight line for measurements that disagree, by making the squared errors as small as possible.

recap.keyIdea: When measurements cannot all be matched, least squares picks the fit with the smallest total of squared residuals. For one constant that fit is the average, and for measurements at x = 0, 1 and 2 the slope is (last y − first y) ÷ 2.

blocks.text: Back with the bolt, you found that 8 cm is the projection of the readings onto (1, 1, 1) and that the residuals of a projection add up to zero. You then fitted a line through the seedling's heights, and used the same idea on a vine and on taxi fares.

recap.nextHook: Fitting the line took two equations solved together, because the columns (1, 1, 1) and (0, 1, 2) are not at right angles to each other. A pair at right angles would split the work in two, and the next lesson shows how to build such a pair from any two vectors.

lessons.title: Build an orthonormal basis

lead.text: Suppose e₁ = (0.6, 0.8) and e₂ = (0.8, −0.6). Both have length 1, since 0.36 + 0.64 = 1, and their dot product is 0.48 − 0.48 = 0, so they meet at a right angle. Take the vector w = (5, 0) and ask how much of each stake it needs. Dot w with each one: w · e₁ = 3 and w · e₂ = 4.

Those two numbers are the answer. Three copies of e₁ plus four copies of e₂ give 3(0.6, 0.8) + 4(0.8, −0.6) = (1.8 + 3.2, 2.4 − 2.4) = (5, 0), which is w. No equations had to be solved. When two directions are at right angles and each has length 1, the amount of each that a vector needs is a single dot product. A basis made of such vectors is called an orthonormal basis.

afterFigure.text: The length of 1 matters. A longer stake would make the dot product overshoot, and it would have to be divided by the length squared, as in the projection formula. Making each length 1 removes that division, so the amount needed is the dot product on its own. The rest of the lesson builds an orthonormal basis from vectors that start out crooked.

lead.text: Start with the simplest straightening. A vector v points to (4, 7): 4 across and 7 up. The x axis can serve as the first stake, with direction (1, 0). The part of v that lies along the axis is its projection, (4, 0), the shadow that v casts on the axis.

Cut that shadow off. What remains is v minus the projection, the residual from the earlier lessons: (4, 7) − (4, 0) = (0, 7). It points straight up, at a right angle to the axis. That is no accident, since the residual of any projection is perpendicular to the line it was projected onto.

afterFigure.text: Here the axis made the arithmetic easy, but the idea works for any direction. Cut the projection onto a first stake off any vector and what is left has nothing along that stake, so it is perpendicular to it. This gives a way to turn a crooked second vector into one at a right angle to the first. What the cut leaves has an arbitrary length, which is the next thing to fix.

lead.text: Removing the part of v that lies along a direction leaves the part that does not. The direction here is the x axis, (1, 0), and v = (3, 1).

reveal.text: You removed the part along the x axis. What is left, (0, 1), points straight up, at a right angle to the direction you removed.

lead.text: Now try a crooked pair with a slanted first vector: u = (4, 3) and v = (3, 5). The first move is to divide u by its length, which is called normalising it, because the first stake of an orthonormal basis needs length 1. The length of u is 5, so e₁ = (0.8, 0.6).

The second move cuts from v its shadow on e₁. Since e₁ has length 1, the shadow is (v · e₁) e₁ with no division. Here v · e₁ = 2.4 + 3 = 5.4, so the shadow is 5.4(0.8, 0.6) = (4.32, 3.24). The residual is (3, 5) − (4.32, 3.24) = (−1.32, 1.76), and it is at a right angle to e₁.

The third move normalises the residual. Its length is √(1.7424 + 3.0976) = √4.84 = 2.2, so e₂ = (−1.32, 1.76) ÷ 2.2 = (−0.6, 0.8). A dot product checks the result: e₁ · e₂ = −0.48 + 0.48 = 0. These moves make up the Gram–Schmidt process. Normalise the first vector. Then cut its shadow off the next vector and normalise what remains.

afterFigure.text: The last move is needed because cutting off a shadow only guarantees a right angle. It says nothing about length, and the residual here came out 2.2 long. A third vector would be handled the same way, with the shadows on both earlier stakes cut off before it is normalised.

cases.label: Shadow of (3, 5) on the x axis

steps.headline: Make an orthonormal pair from (3, 4) and (1, 0).

workedSteps.text: Divide the first vector by its length, 5.
Subtract the projection of (1, 0) onto e₁. The dot product is 0.6.
The residual has length 0.8. Divide by it to get a unit vector.

steps.headline: Normalise (1, 1). Find its first coordinate as a decimal.

workedSteps.text: Find the length.
Divide the first coordinate by √2. What is it as a decimal?

lead.text: The vector is (−3, 4). Find its length, then divide the coordinate the question asks for.

reveal.text: You divided by the length, and the result has length 1. Normalising keeps the direction and fixes the size.

lead.text: The process can fail, and the failure tells you something. Take u = (1, 2) and v = (3, 6). Normalise u to get e₁ = (1, 2) ÷ √5. The shadow of v on e₁ is (v · e₁) e₁ = (15 ÷ √5)(1, 2) ÷ √5 = 3(1, 2) = (3, 6), which is all of v, so the residual is (0, 0).

Here v is already a multiple of u, so the two vectors never pointed in different directions. Nothing is left after the cut, and the zero vector cannot be divided by its length to give a vector of length 1. This is why Gram–Schmidt needs independent vectors. A vector that lies along an earlier one adds no new direction, so the process stops with fewer vectors than it started with.

afterFigure.text: When the vectors are independent, every step leaves something behind. Two independent vectors in the plane always give an orthonormal basis of the plane, and the first stake can be any direction you like. A basis chosen this way is a set of axes you picked yourself. The next lesson looks for axes that a matrix picks out on its own.

lead.text: Take u = (1, 1) and v = (2, 2). Cut from v its shadow on u, then see whether anything is left to make a second basis vector.

lessons.orientation: Subtract projections and normalise the remaining independent directions.

blocks.text: Fitting the seedling's line took two equations that had to be solved together, because the columns (1, 1, 1) and (0, 1, 2) lean on each other. Their dot product is 3, so the amount of one column you need depends on how much of the other you use.

Directions at right angles do not interfere like that. Picture two stakes in a field, one pointing east and one pointing north. To describe the way to a flagpole you say how far east and how far north, and the two answers are independent: changing one does nothing to the other. Stakes that lean towards each other lose this, because walking along one also carries you part of the way along the other.

Most pairs of directions are crooked. This lesson takes any two crooked vectors and straightens them, one step at a time, into two vectors at right angles that each have length 1. The first stays where it is, and the second is trimmed until it stands square to it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn two independent vectors into two perpendicular unit vectors, step by step.

recap.keyIdea: Gram–Schmidt builds an orthonormal basis from independent vectors. The first is normalised. Each later one has its shadows on the earlier vectors cut off, and what is left is normalised.

blocks.text: You started with crooked pairs and straightened them. You cut the shadow off (4, 7), built e₁ and e₂ from (4, 3) and (3, 5), and saw that (3, 6) leaves nothing after the cut because it lies along (1, 2).

recap.nextHook: An orthonormal basis is a set of axes that you choose yourself. A matrix has axes of its own, which are directions it only stretches. The next lesson shows how to find them.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues

steps.headline: What a matrix does to an arrow

lead.text: A matrix acts on an arrow by multiplying it, so a 2 × 2 matrix A takes an arrow v and gives a new arrow A v. Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$, with rows (3, 1) and (0, 2). Dot each row with v = (0, 1) and you get A v = (1, 2). The arrow that pointed straight up now leans to the right, so it has been turned as well as stretched.

Try v = (1, 1) and the result is (4, 2), which leans a different way from (1, 1). Most arrows are turned like this. Now try v = (1, 0). The rows give A v = (3, 0), so the arrow still lies along the x axis. It has become three times as long and has not turned at all.

afterFigure.text: So this matrix has at least one arrow that keeps its line. The figure checks a candidate arrow. When the output lies on the same line as the input, it reports the stretch factor, and when it does not, it reports nothing. The next screen gives these special arrows a name and says exactly what the test is.

lead.text: An arrow that keeps its line is described by one equation, A v = λv. On the left is what the machine does to v. On the right is v multiplied by a plain number λ, the Greek letter lambda. The equation says that the output is a multiple of the input. A nonzero vector v that satisfies it is called an eigenvector of A, and the number λ is its eigenvalue.

Back to the matrix from the last screen. The arrow (1, 0) satisfies A v = 3v, so it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3. A second one has been hiding. For v = (1, −1) the rows give A v = (3 − 1, 0 − 2) = (2, −2), which is 2 times (1, −1). So (1, −1) is an eigenvector too, with eigenvalue 2. Along the first the machine stretches by 3, and along the second by 2.

afterFigure.text: The word nonzero matters. The zero arrow stays at zero whatever the machine does, so it would satisfy the equation for every λ and tell us nothing. Every other arrow is a fair candidate, and the test is always the same: work out A v and see whether it is a multiple of v.

lead.text: A machine turns the arrow (1, 2) into the arrow (4, 8). Compare the output with the input, one coordinate at a time.

reveal.text: You found that each output coordinate is the same multiple of the input one. That shared multiple is the eigenvalue.

lead.text: The eigenvalue can be any number, and its size says what happens along that line. A value above 1, like the 3 above, stretches the arrow. Between 0 and 1 the arrow shrinks towards the centre. At exactly 1 it is left as it was.

A negative eigenvalue makes the output point the opposite way along the same line. Take the matrix with rows (−1, 0) and (0, 2) and the arrow (1, 0). The rows give (−1, 0), which is −1 times (1, 0). The arrow keeps its line, but it lands on the other side of the centre.

An eigenvalue of 0 is allowed too. The matrix with rows (1, 1) and (1, 1) sends (1, −1) to (1 − 1, 1 − 1) = (0, 0). The output is the zero vector, which is 0 times (1, −1), so (1, −1) is still an eigenvector, now with eigenvalue 0. Only the eigenvector itself has to be nonzero. The machine is allowed to crush it to nothing.

reveal.text: You found the output points opposite to the input. A negative eigenvalue flips the direction along that line.

lead.text: Not every arrow is an eigenvector, and the test shows when one is not. Return to A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ and try the candidate (1, 1). The output A v = (4, 2) would have to be λ times (1, 1), which needs both entries to match. They are 4 and 2, so the output leans a different way from the input and (1, 1) is not an eigenvector.

As a rule, work out A v, divide one output entry by the matching input entry to get a trial λ, and check that the other entry gives the same number. If the two disagree, the arrow has been turned. When an input entry is 0, divide using the other entry instead.

A 2 × 2 matrix often has two lines of eigenvectors, as this one does, along (1, 0) and (1, −1). Two such lines are two axes of the machine's own. The next lesson uses them in place of the usual x and y axes, and finds that the matrix then turns into plain stretching.

blocks.text: Think of a sheet of rubber with a grid drawn on it, pinned at the centre. A machine pulls and squeezes the sheet. Most of the arrows you could draw from the centre come out pointing somewhere new, because the machine drags them sideways as it stretches them.

Look closely and a few arrows behave differently. They come out lying along the line they started on, only longer or shorter. If you wanted to describe what the machine does, these arrows would be the easiest place to start, because its effect on them is a single number, the stretch.
The last lesson showed how to choose axes of your own. This lesson looks for the axes the machine chooses. It shows how to test whether an arrow keeps its line, and what the stretch along it means.

recap.keyIdea: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector that a matrix only scales: A v = λv. The scale factor λ is its eigenvalue, and it may be negative or zero.

blocks.text: You applied a matrix to arrows and saw that most of them turn. You tested arrows with A v = λv, found the factors 3, 2, 5, 1 and −2, and saw that (1, 0) is not an eigenvector of the matrix with rows (2, 1) and (1, 2).

recap.nextHook: A matrix with two lines of eigenvectors turns into two plain stretches when you use those lines as axes. The next lesson shows how to write that down.

lessons.title: Diagonalise a map

steps.headline: Splitting an arrow along the eigenvectors

lead.text: Take the machine from the opening and a different arrow, (0, 2). Along the machine's two lines it is (0, 2) = (1, 1) − (1, −1). That is one copy of the first eigenvector and minus one copy of the second. The eigenvectors are independent, which makes them a basis of the plane, so every arrow can be written as a mix of them.

Now apply the machine to the pieces. It triples the first piece, giving 3(1, 1) = (3, 3). It leaves the second as it was, so minus one copy of (1, −1) stays minus one copy. Adding the results gives (3, 3) − (1, −1) = (2, 4). A matrix acts on a sum by acting on each part and adding, so (2, 4) is the machine's output for (0, 2).

afterFigure.text: That gives a recipe that works for any arrow. First write it as a mix of the eigenvectors. Each part is then multiplied by its own eigenvalue, and the results are added. The only real work is finding the mix, and the next screens turn that work into a matrix.

lead.text: The machine triples every arrow along (1, 1) and leaves every arrow along (1, −1) unchanged. The arrow (2, 0) is (1, 1) + (1, −1).

reveal.text: You tripled the first piece and kept the second: 3(1, 1) + (1, −1) = (4, 2). Its first coordinate is 4.

steps.headline: Writing the matrix as P D P⁻¹

lead.text: The same idea can be written as a product of matrices. Take A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ with rows (3, 1) and (0, 2). Its eigenvectors are (1, 0) with eigenvalue 3 and (1, −1) with eigenvalue 2. Let P be the matrix whose columns are those eigenvectors, (1, 0) and (1, −1). Let D hold the eigenvalues in the same order along its diagonal, with 3 and 2 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere. A matrix with nonzero entries only on its diagonal is a diagonal matrix.

Then A = P D P⁻¹. Read the product from the right, because the rightmost matrix acts first. P⁻¹ turns an arrow into its mix of eigenvectors, telling us how many copies of each are needed. D multiplies each count by its eigenvalue. P then builds the arrow out of the scaled eigenvectors. For the arrow (4, 2), P⁻¹ gives the counts 6 and −2, D turns them into 18 and −4, and P builds 18(1, 0) − 4(1, −1) = (14, 4). Applying A to (4, 2) directly gives (14, 4) too.

afterFigure.text: Writing A this way is called diagonalising A. All the machine's complexity sits in P and P⁻¹, which only change coordinates, and D does the real work as a plain stretch along each axis. It needs the eigenvectors to be independent, so that P has an inverse. The next screens put the form to use.

lead.text: A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Each diagonal entry of D is the eigenvalue of the matching column of P. Work out A v for the first column of P to find it.

reveal.text: You found the eigenvalue of the first column of P. That number sits in the first diagonal slot of D.

steps.headline: Applying a matrix again and again

lead.text: Suppose the machine is used twice in a row. Apply A to an eigenvector v with eigenvalue λ and you get λv. The second application acts on λv. Since a matrix acts on a multiple by acting on the original and multiplying, A(λv) = λ(A v) = λ·λv = λ²v. Each application multiplies the arrow by λ once more, so n applications multiply it by λⁿ.

Take A with rows (3, 1) and (0, 2) and the eigenvector (1, 0), which has eigenvalue 3. Three applications give 3³ = 27 times (1, 0). Checking by hand: A(1, 0) = (3, 0), then A(3, 0) = (9, 0), then A(9, 0) = (27, 0). Repeating a matrix on a general arrow takes many multiplications, but in the eigenvector basis it takes powers of plain numbers.

In matrix form, A² = P D P⁻¹ P D P⁻¹. The P⁻¹ P in the middle cancels to the identity, so A² = P D² P⁻¹. Squaring D means squaring each diagonal entry. In general Aⁿ = P Dⁿ P⁻¹, which reduces a hundredfold repetition to raising two numbers to the power 100.

steps.headline: Apply $\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ twice to its eigenvector (1, 1), which has eigenvalue 5.

workedSteps.text: One application multiplies by 5.
The second application multiplies by 5 again.

steps.headline: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 1), find the scalar that multiplies v in A²v.

workedSteps.text: This eigenvector has eigenvalue 3, so A v = 3v.
Apply A again. What scalar multiplies v in A²v?

lead.text: A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 0), which has eigenvalue 2. Each application of A multiplies v by that eigenvalue.

reveal.text: You multiplied by the eigenvalue once per application. After n applications the scalar is λ to the power n.

steps.headline: When it cannot be done, and when the order changes

lead.text: A matrix does not always have two independent eigenvectors, and then P⁻¹ does not exist. Take the shear with rows (1, 1) and (0, 1). It sends (1, 0) to (1, 0), so (1, 0) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. For a general arrow (a, b) the output is (a + b, b), which is a multiple of (a, b) only when b = 0. Every eigenvector lies along the x axis.

afterFigure.text: P needs two independent columns, because an invertible matrix has columns that form a basis of the plane. With both columns along the x axis, P would flatten the plane onto a line and could not be undone. So this shear cannot be diagonalised with real numbers, and the test is to count the independent eigenvectors.

The order of the columns is free as long as D follows it. For the matrix with rows (3, 1) and (0, 2), putting (1, −1) before (1, 0) in P means putting 2 before 3 in D. Each eigenvalue stays beside its own eigenvector, and the product is still A.

lead.text: Reorder the columns of P and the entries of D must reorder with them. Each eigenvalue stays beside its own eigenvector. Now (1, −1) is the first column of P.

lessons.orientation: Use an eigenvector basis to separate a square map into independent scalings.

blocks.text: A machine acts on every arrow in the plane, and two kinds of arrow are easy to describe. It triples every arrow along (1, 1), and it leaves every arrow along (1, −1) exactly as it was. Those are two lines of eigenvectors, with eigenvalues 3 and 1.

Most arrows lie along neither line. The arrow (2, 0) points along the x axis, for instance. It can still be built from the two easy ones, because (2, 0) = (1, 1) + (1, −1). Since the machine treats each part so simply, its effect on the whole arrow should follow from its effect on the parts.

This lesson follows that thought. The plan is to split an arrow along the machine's own lines and scale each part. Then the parts go back together. Doing this gives a way of writing the matrix itself as a product of three simpler ones, and it makes repeating the machine a hundred times about as easy as doing it once.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write a matrix as P D P⁻¹ and use D to apply that matrix again and again.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix with a basis of eigenvectors is P D P⁻¹. P's columns are the eigenvectors and D holds their eigenvalues in the same order, so powers act as λⁿ.

blocks.text: You split arrows along eigenvectors and scaled each part. The matrix with rows (2, 1) and (1, 2) gave 3 and 1 on the diagonal of D, and applying it twice multiplied (1, 1) by 9. A shear showed why some matrices have no P.

recap.nextHook: Diagonalising needs a square matrix with enough eigenvectors, and many matrices fall short of that. The next lesson shows that every matrix, even a rectangular one, splits into a turn, a stretch and a second turn.

lessons.title: Singular value decomposition

lead.text: Take the machine from the opening and follow arrows of length 1 through it. The arrow (1, 0) points across. The stretch makes it 5 long, and the quarter turn swings it to point straight up, still 5 long. The arrow (0, 1) points up. The stretch makes it 3 long, and the turn lays it flat, still 3 long. A turn changes where an arrow points and never how long it is.

Arrows between those two are stretched by amounts between 3 and 5, depending on how far they lean towards each axis. All the arrows of length 1 together form a circle. After the stretch the circle has become an oval, 5 across and 3 up, and the turn leaves the oval's size alone and only rotates it. So the longest output the machine can produce from an input of length 1 is the long side of the oval, and the shortest is the short side.

afterFigure.text: The two lengths, 5 and 3, describe the machine's stretching completely. The turn only decides which way the oval ends up pointing. Every matrix has a pair of numbers like this. The next screen gives them a name and says how a matrix is written in terms of them.

lead.text: A different machine stretches every arrow across by 4 and up by 2, then spins the whole plane. Think about the oval that a circle of length-1 arrows becomes.

reveal.text: A turn keeps lengths, so the longest output comes from the biggest stretch, which is 4.

lead.text: The machine in the opening was a stretch followed by a turn. The general case allows a turn before the stretch as well, because the axes along which a matrix stretches need not be the axes the input came with. Every matrix A can be written as A = U Σ Vᵀ. Read it from the right. The input meets Vᵀ first, which turns it. The stretch Σ comes next, and U turns the result once more.

U and V are orthogonal matrices, which means they only turn or flip the plane and never change a length. Σ, the Greek capital sigma, is a diagonal matrix, and the numbers on its diagonal are the stretch sizes. These numbers are the singular values of A. For the machine in the opening they are 5 and 3, listed from largest to smallest as is usual.

afterFigure.text: Singular values are never negative. The matrix with rows (−5, 0) and (0, 1) flips the x axis as well as stretching it, but a flip is a kind of turn, so it goes into U or V and Σ keeps only the sizes. A shortcut helps for matrices like these: when the columns of A are at right angles to each other, the singular values are simply the lengths of the columns.

lead.text: A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$ stretches across by 3 and up by 2, and flips up. Singular values record only the sizes of the stretches.

reveal.text: You compared the sizes of the stretches and ignored the flip. Singular values measure size only.

workedSteps.text: The two columns are perpendicular. Their lengths are the stretch sizes.
The minus sign is a flip, so it goes into U. Σ keeps only the sizes.

lead.text: A singular value can be zero. Take the matrix with every entry 1, rows (1, 1) and (1, 1). Both columns equal (1, 1), so the machine sends every arrow (a, b) to (a + b, a + b), which lies on a single line. The plane has been flattened onto that line. The singular values are 2 and 0: the machine stretches the arrow (1, 1) by 2, and it crushes the perpendicular arrow (1, −1) to nothing.

This links back to rank. The rank of a matrix counts the independent directions it keeps, and each kept direction has a stretch above zero. So the number of positive singular values equals the rank. A rank-one matrix has one positive singular value and the rest zero. A square matrix with determinant 0 has at least one singular value equal to 0, which is the flattening seen earlier.

steps.headline: Find the smaller singular value of $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: The second row is twice the first, so the rank is 1.
The number of positive singular values equals the rank. What is the smaller singular value?

lead.text: A matrix need not be square. A 3 × 2 matrix takes arrows with two entries and gives arrows with three entries, so it carries the plane into three-dimensional space. Take the matrix with rows (3, 0), (0, 1) and (0, 0). The arrow (1, 0) goes to (3, 0, 0), and (0, 1) goes to (0, 1, 0). The columns are at right angles and have lengths 3 and 1, so those are the singular values.

The three factors change shape to fit. Vᵀ is 2 × 2, because it turns the plane of inputs, and U is 3 × 3, because it turns the space of outputs. Σ must carry two inputs to three outputs, so it is 3 × 2: the singular values 3 and 1 sit on its diagonal and a row of zeros fills the bottom. Σ always has the same shape as A, and a matrix has as many singular values as the smaller of its two sizes.
The matrix has rows (1, 0, 0) and (0, 2, 0). Its columns are (1, 0), (0, 2) and (0, 0). Read the stretches from the columns that are not zero.

reveal.text: You read the stretches off the matrix and took the smaller. Singular values are usually listed from the largest to the smallest.

lead.text: Now the other shape. A 2 × 3 matrix takes three inputs to two outputs. Think about what shape Σ needs so that it does the same job as A.

lessons.orientation: Separate a rectangular map into orthogonal coordinate changes and nonnegative stretches.

blocks.text: Diagonalising worked for matrices with enough eigenvectors, and it left some matrices out: the rectangular ones, and square ones such as the shear. This lesson shows that a machine can be described plainly even for those, and that the description uses only turns and stretches.

Start with a machine that works in two stages. The first stage makes arrows 5 times as long across and 3 times as long up. The second spins the plane through a quarter turn. Now feed in a circle of arrows of length 1 and look at the shape that comes out: an oval, 5 across and 3 up, turned onto its side. The spin cannot change the oval's shape, only the way it points.
That picture holds for every matrix, with a turn before the stretch as well as after it. The sizes of the stretches are the numbers that matter most, and they are the subject of this lesson.

intro.promise: By the end you'll split any matrix into two length-preserving turns and one stretch, and read its singular values.

recap.keyIdea: Every matrix is A = U Σ Vᵀ. U and Vᵀ preserve length, and Σ holds the nonnegative singular values: the stretches. The number of positive ones is the rank.

blocks.text: You followed a circle of arrows through a stretch and a turn and saw an oval come out. You read the largest singular value of the matrix with rows (3, 0) and (0, −2) as 3, found that a rank-one matrix has a singular value of 0, and matched the shape of Σ to A.

recap.nextHook: That completes the course. Every matrix, from a single column to a rectangle, now has a plain description as turns and stretches, and a fresh problem will bring these ideas back when you review them later.
